25442.m: Copernicus realised that the Earth goes around the Sun.

25443.q: As Copernicus explained, what causes day and night?
a: The Earth spins on its axis
25443.e: The Earth spins once a day on its own axis. The side facing the Sun has day.
25443.m: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.

25444.q: What on the Moon bears Copernicus’s name?
25444.e: Many craters on the Moon are named after famous scientists. The crater Copernicus can even be seen with binoculars.
25444.m: A crater on the Moon is named after Copernicus.

25445.q: Which force makes an apple fall from a tree to the ground?
25445.e: The Earth pulls all things towards it. Isaac Newton described this force precisely.
25445.m: Gravity pulls things towards the Earth.

25446.q: What did Newton explain with the Moon’s pull?
25446.e: The Moon pulls on the water of the seas. That is why the sea rises and falls twice a day on many coasts.

25447.q: At which famous English university did Newton study and teach?
25447.e: Newton studied at Cambridge and became a professor of mathematics there. He stayed at this university for many years.
25447.m: Newton did his research at the University of Cambridge.

25448.q: According to Newton, what keeps the Moon on its path around the Earth?
25448.e: Newton realised that the same force that makes the apple fall also holds the Moon in place. Without it, the Moon would fly away.
25448.m: Gravity keeps the Moon near the Earth.

25449.q: What did Newton split white light into using a glass prism?
25449.e: Newton let sunlight pass through a prism. Behind it, all the colours of the rainbow appeared.
25449.m: White light is made of all the colours of the rainbow.

25451.q: Which telescope did Newton build with a mirror instead of glass lenses?
25451.e: Around 1668 Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror. Large telescopes still work like this today.

25452.q: Why can an astronaut jump much higher on the Moon than on the Earth?
a: There is a strong wind there
25452.e: The Moon is much smaller than the Earth and pulls less strongly. That is why you weigh less there.
25452.m: Gravity is weaker on the Moon.

25453.q: What did Johannes Kepler describe with his famous laws?
25453.e: Kepler calculated exactly how the planets move around the Sun. His laws still apply today.
25453.m: Kepler described the orbits of the planets.

25454.q: According to Kepler, what shape are the planets’ orbits?
25454.e: Before Kepler, people thought planets moved in exact circles. Kepler showed that they are ellipses, that is, slightly stretched circles.
25454.m: Planets orbit the Sun in ellipses.

25455.q: Which country did Johannes Kepler come from?
25455.e: Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in Württemberg. That is in present-day Germany.

25456.q: Which astronomer from Denmark did Kepler work with in Prague?
25456.e: Tycho Brahe had observed the planets very precisely. Kepler used his measurements for his laws.

25457.q: What did the space telescope named after Kepler look for?
25457.e: The Kepler space telescope launched in 2009. It found thousands of planets orbiting other stars.
25457.m: The Kepler telescope looked for planets around other stars.

25458.q: What did Kepler improve so that people could observe the sky better?
25458.e: Kepler suggested a telescope with two curved lenses. It shows a bigger image than the older telescope.

25459.q: According to Kepler, when does a planet move fastest?
a: When it is close to the Sun
When it is far from the Sun
When it is night on Earth
25459.e: Kepler found that planets move faster near the Sun. Further away they slow down.
25459.m: Planets are faster when close to the Sun.

25460.q: What did Johannes Kepler mainly study?
25460.e: Kepler was an astronomer. He calculated how the planets move around the Sun.
25460.m: Kepler studied the orbits of the planets.

25461.q: Which animal did Albrecht Dürer paint so realistically in 1502 that you can see every hair?
25461.e: The picture is called “Young Hare”. It is one of the most famous animal pictures in the world.
25461.m: Dürer painted a very realistic hare.

25462.q: Which famous drawing by Dürer shows two hands?
25462.e: “Praying Hands” is a drawing by Dürer. Today you can find it on many cards and pictures.

25463.q: Whom did Dürer paint again and again, as one of the first artists to do so?
25463.e: Dürer painted several self-portraits. That was something new at the time.
25463.m: Dürer painted many pictures of himself.

25464.q: Which technique allowed Dürer to print a picture many times?
25464.e: For a woodcut, the picture is carved into a wooden block. Afterwards it can be printed on paper again and again.
25464.m: With a woodcut, pictures can be printed many times.

25465.q: Which animal did Dürer draw in 1515, even though he had never seen one himself?
25465.e: Dürer only had a description and a sketch. That is why his rhinoceros wears a kind of armour.
25465.m: Dürer drew a rhinoceros without ever having seen one.

25466.q: Which country did Dürer travel to in order to get to know the new art of the Renaissance?
25466.e: Dürer travelled over the Alps to Venice. There he learned a lot from the Italian painters.
25466.m: Dürer got to know the Renaissance in Italy.

25467.q: In which Swiss city did the young Dürer work around 1492?
25467.e: As a young journeyman, Dürer travelled around. In Basel he made pictures for printed books.
25467.m: The young Dürer worked in Basel.

25468.q: With which two letters did Dürer sign his works?
25468.e: Dürer put a large A with a small D underneath on his pictures. That is his mark.
25468.m: Dürer signed with the letters AD.

25469.q: With which device did Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discover tiny living things?
25469.e: Leeuwenhoek built small microscopes himself. With them he saw things you cannot see with the naked eye.
25469.m: Leeuwenhoek did his research with a microscope.

25470.q: Which country did Leeuwenhoek come from?
25470.e: Leeuwenhoek lived in the town of Delft. It is in the Netherlands.

25471.q: What did Leeuwenhoek see when he looked at a drop of water under the microscope?
25471.e: Lots of tiny creatures were swimming in the drop. He called them “little animals”.
25471.m: Tiny living things live in a drop of water.

25472.q: What job did Leeuwenhoek have before he became famous?
25472.e: Leeuwenhoek sold fabrics. He checked the threads with magnifying glasses, and that is how he came to the microscope.
25472.m: Leeuwenhoek was originally a cloth merchant.

a: It makes small things look big
It makes distant things look close
25473.e: A microscope magnifies very small things. That way you can look at them closely.

25474.q: What did Leeuwenhoek find in the plaque on his teeth?
25474.e: He scraped plaque off his teeth and saw tiny living things. Today we know they were bacteria.

25475.q: How many lenses did most of Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes have?
25475.e: His microscopes usually had only one tiny, very finely ground lens. Even so, some magnified more than 200 times.
25475.m: Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes had only one lens.

25476.q: What did Leeuwenhoek observe in blood?
25476.e: Leeuwenhoek described red blood cells very precisely. They give blood its red colour.
25476.m: Red blood cells float in the blood.

25477.q: Into which language did Martin Luther translate the Bible?
25477.e: Before that, the Bible in church was mostly in Latin. Luther wanted everyone to be able to read it.
25477.m: Luther translated the Bible into German.

25478.q: Which invention helped spread Luther’s writings quickly everywhere?
25478.e: With printing, Luther’s Bible and writings could be produced quickly in large numbers. Johannes Gutenberg had invented it around 1450.

25479.q: From which language did Luther translate the New Testament?
25479.e: The New Testament was originally written in Greek. Luther translated from this text.
25479.m: Luther translated the New Testament from Greek.

25480.q: Roughly how long did Luther take to translate the New Testament?
25480.e: Luther worked very fast and was finished after about eleven weeks. For the whole Bible, he and his helpers needed many years.
25480.m: Luther translated the New Testament in about eleven weeks.

25481.q: How did Luther want to translate so that everyone would understand him?
25481.e: Luther said you had to listen to how ordinary people really talk. He chose words that everyone knew.
25481.m: Luther translated into the language of the people.

25482.q: Under which false name did Luther live in hiding at the castle?
25482.e: Luther let his hair and beard grow. As “Junker Jörg”, nobody recognised him.

25483.q: According to legend, what did Luther throw at the Devil in the castle?
25483.e: That is what an old legend says. The story is probably made up, but it is very well known.
25483.m: According to legend, Luther threw an inkpot at the Devil.

25484.q: Which reformer in Zurich also published a Bible in German?
25484.e: In 1531 the whole Bible was published in German in Zurich. Zwingli and his helpers had translated it.
25484.m: Zwingli published a German Bible in Zurich.

25485.q: Who is considered the inventor of the pocket watch?
25485.e: Around 1510 the locksmith Peter Henlein built small clocks that people could carry around. That is why he is considered the inventor of the pocket watch.
25485.m: Peter Henlein is considered the inventor of the pocket watch.

25486.q: Where did men use to carry their pocket watch?
25486.e: The pocket watch was usually kept in a small pocket of the waistcoat. You took it out to read the time.
25486.m: The pocket watch was kept in the waistcoat pocket.

25487.q: What was a pocket watch attached to so that it would not get lost?
25487.e: The watch was kept in the waistcoat pocket. A chain connected it to the clothes.
25487.m: A pocket watch often hangs on a chain.

25488.q: What powers a mechanical pocket watch?
25488.e: Inside the watch there is a spring that you wind up. As it unwinds, it moves the hands.
25488.m: A spring powers a mechanical watch.

25489.q: What did you regularly have to do with an old pocket watch to keep it going?
25489.e: To wind it, you turn a little wheel called the crown. Otherwise the watch stops after a while.
25489.m: An old pocket watch has to be wound up.

25490.q: Which two towns in the canton of Neuchâtel are World Heritage Sites because of watchmaking?
25490.e: Both towns were built entirely around the needs of watchmakers. They have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2009.
25490.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are watchmaking towns.

25491.q: In which region of Switzerland have there long been especially many watchmakers?
25491.e: Many watch workshops grew up in the Jura arc from Geneva to Basel. Swiss watches are famous all over the world.
25491.m: There are many watchmakers in the Jura.

25492.q: Which kind of watch later replaced the pocket watch?
25492.e: In the 20th century more and more people wore their watch on their wrist. That was more practical than in a pocket.
25492.m: The wristwatch replaced the pocket watch.

25493.q: Which country did William Shakespeare come from?
25493.e: Shakespeare was an English writer. He lived and worked mainly in London.

25494.q: In which small town was Shakespeare born?
25494.e: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564. You can visit the house where he was born today.

25495.q: Which play by Shakespeare tells the story of a young couple in love from Verona?
25495.e: Romeo and Juliet love each other, but their families are enemies. The story is very sad.
25495.m: Romeo and Juliet is a play by Shakespeare.

25496.q: What was the name of the famous round theatre in London where Shakespeare’s plays were performed?
25496.e: The Globe Theatre was a round wooden theatre. A reconstruction stands in London again today.
25496.m: Shakespeare’s plays were performed at the Globe Theatre.

25497.e: Shakespeare wrote comedies, tragedies and poems. His plays are performed all over the world.

25498.q: Which play does the line “To be, or not to be” come from?
25498.e: Prince Hamlet says this line while he is thinking. It is one of the best-known lines in the world.
25498.m: The line “To be, or not to be” comes from Hamlet.

25499.q: In which play by Shakespeare do fairies get up to mischief in a magic forest?
25499.e: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” features fairies and a sprite called Puck. It is a funny comedy.
25499.m: Fairies appear in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

25500.q: In Shakespeare’s time, who played the female roles in the theatre?
25500.e: Women were not allowed to act on stage in England at that time. So boys took the female roles.
25500.m: In Shakespeare’s time, boys played the female roles.

25501.q: Which country did the painter Raphael come from?
25501.e: Raphael was born in Urbino in Italy in 1483. Later he painted in Florence and Rome.
25501.m: Raphael was a painter from Italy.

25502.q: Which famous wall painting by Raphael shows many scholars of ancient Greece?
25502.e: In the painting, thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle stand in a great hall. It is one of the most famous wall paintings in the world.
25502.m: Raphael painted The School of Athens.

25503.q: What can you see right at the bottom of Raphael’s painting “Sistine Madonna”?
25503.e: The two thoughtful little angels are world-famous. You can find them on many postcards.
25503.m: Two angels sit at the bottom of the Sistine Madonna.

25504.q: What did Raphael paint especially often?
25504.e: Raphael painted many Madonnas, that is, pictures of Mary with the baby Jesus. They look gentle and kind.
25504.m: Raphael painted many pictures of Mary with the child.

25505.q: How old was Raphael when he died?
25505.e: Raphael lived from 1483 to 1520. So he died at only 37.

25506.q: For whom did Raphael decorate magnificent rooms in the Vatican?
25506.e: The Pope brought Raphael to Rome. Today the rooms are called the “Raphael Rooms”.
25506.m: Raphael decorated rooms for the Pope.

25507.q: Which two artists, together with Raphael, are counted among the greatest painters of the High Renaissance?
25507.e: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael lived at the same time. All three worked in Italy.
25507.m: Raphael, Leonardo and Michelangelo are great masters.

25508.e: His father, Giovanni Santi, was a painter and poet. Raphael learned from him from an early age.
25508.m: Raphael’s father was a painter too.

25509.e: The word comes from French. It refers to a rebirth of ancient knowledge.

25510.q: Which ancient art did people admire again during the Renaissance?
a: The art of the ancient Greeks and Romans
The art of the ancient Egyptians
25510.e: People admired the works of antiquity again. Artists and scholars learned from the ancient Greeks and Romans.
25510.m: In the Renaissance, the art of antiquity came back to life.

25511.q: Which invention around 1450 helped spread new knowledge quickly?
25511.e: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type. Now books could be produced much faster.

25512.q: Which rich banking family supported many artists during the Renaissance?
25512.e: The Medici were very rich bankers. They gave artists commissions and money.

25513.q: Who painted the famous picture “Mona Lisa”?
25513.e: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, inventor and scientist. The Mona Lisa now hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
25513.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

25514.e: The Renaissance lasted roughly from the 15th into the 16th century. That is about 200 years.
25514.m: The Renaissance was roughly from 1400 to 1600.

25515.q: What did Renaissance painters learn so that their pictures would look three-dimensional and deep?
25515.e: With perspective, things further back are painted smaller. This makes a flat picture look deep.

25516.q: Which period came directly before the Renaissance?
25516.e: Before the Renaissance came the Middle Ages. The early modern period begins with the Renaissance.
25516.m: The Middle Ages came before the Renaissance.

25517.q: Which famous Renaissance painter worked in Basel for a long time?
25517.e: In Basel, Holbein painted portraits and altarpieces. Many of his works hang in the Kunstmuseum Basel today.
25517.m: Hans Holbein the Younger worked in Basel.

25518.q: Which country did Louis XIV rule?
25518.e: Louis XIV was King of France. He belonged to the Bourbon family.
25518.m: Louis XIV was King of France.

25519.q: Under Louis XIV, who decided almost everything in France alone?
25519.e: Louis XIV ruled as an absolute monarch. He made the important decisions alone, and nobody was allowed to contradict him.
25519.m: Louis XIV ruled France almost entirely on his own.

25520.q: In which country is the Palace of Versailles?
25520.e: The Palace of Versailles is in France. It is one of the most famous palaces in the world.
25520.m: The Palace of Versailles is in France.

25521.q: What lies all around the Palace of Versailles?
25521.e: Behind the palace is a huge garden with paths, ponds and many fountains. It was laid out very neatly and in straight lines.
25521.m: Versailles is surrounded by a large park with many fountains.

25522.q: Apart from the royal family, who lived in the Palace of Versailles?
25522.e: Louis XIV brought many nobles to his court at Versailles. On top of that there were thousands of servants, cooks and craftsmen.
25522.m: Many nobles and servants lived at the court of Versailles.

25523.q: What did fine gentlemen at the court of Louis XIV wear on their heads?
25523.e: At court, fine gentlemen wore long, curly wigs. That was the great fashion of the time.
25523.m: Fine gentlemen wore large curly wigs back then.

25524.q: What was often used to make wigs white?
25524.e: Wigs were dusted with powder, often made from starch or flour. This made them white or grey.

25525.q: What did a large, expensive wig show other people?
a: That someone was rich and important
25525.e: Large wigs were expensive and took a lot of work. Anyone wearing one showed that they were rich and important.

a: A wide skirt with hoops underneath
25526.e: Round hoops are sewn in underneath a hoop skirt. This makes the skirt stand out wide from the body.
25526.m: A hoop skirt is a wide skirt with hoops.

25527.q: What did fine ladies wear tightly around their upper body under their dress?
25527.e: A corset was laced up tightly. This made the waist look especially slim.
25527.m: A corset made the waist look slim.

25528.q: What colour were the heels on Louis XIV’s shoes?
25528.e: Louis XIV wore shoes with red heels. Only he and nobles he allowed could wear such shoes.
25528.m: Louis XIV wore shoes with red heels.

25529.q: In which present-day country is Mozart’s home town?
25529.e: Salzburg is in Austria today. That is why Mozart is regarded as a famous Austrian composer.
25529.m: Mozart’s home town is in Austria.

25530.q: About how old was Mozart when he wrote his first pieces of music?
25530.e: Mozart was already writing little pieces at about 5 years old. That is why he is called a child prodigy.
25530.m: Mozart was a musical child prodigy.

25531.q: What was Mozart’s older sister, who made music with him, called?
25531.e: His sister Maria Anna was called Nannerl. The two children played together for kings and princes.
25531.m: Mozart’s sister Nannerl made music with him.

25532.q: Who was Mozart’s father and first music teacher?
25532.e: Leopold Mozart was a musician himself. He taught his children and travelled around Europe with them.
25532.m: Leopold Mozart was Wolfgang’s father and teacher.

25533.q: Which Swiss city did the young Mozart visit on a journey in 1766?
25533.e: On their way home in 1766 the Mozart family also travelled through Switzerland. They gave concerts in Zurich, for example.
25533.m: The young Mozart gave concerts in Zurich in 1766.

25534.q: Which well-known piece of music is by Mozart?
25534.e: Mozart wrote “Eine kleine Nachtmusik” (A Little Night Music) in 1787. Many people know its cheerful tune.

25535.q: Which present-day country did Johann Sebastian Bach come from?
25535.e: Bach was born in Eisenach, a town in present-day Germany. He lived and worked in German lands all his life.
25535.m: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer.

25536.q: For which large church instrument is Bach especially famous?
25536.e: Bach was a brilliant organist. He wrote many pieces for the church organ.

25537.q: Roughly how many children did Johann Sebastian Bach have?
25537.e: Bach had 20 children with his two wives. But many of them died as babies.

25538.q: In which city did Bach work for a long time as cantor of St Thomas Church?
25538.e: From 1723 Bach was cantor of St Thomas in Leipzig. There he led the boys’ choir and wrote music for church services.
25538.m: Bach was cantor of St Thomas in Leipzig.

25539.q: Which famous work for the Christmas season did Bach write?
25539.e: The Christmas Oratorio tells the story of Jesus’s birth through music. Bach wrote it in 1734. “Messiah” was written by Handel.

25540.q: In which year was Johann Sebastian Bach born?
25540.e: Bach was born on 21 March 1685. So he lived over 300 years ago.
25540.m: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in 1685.

25541.q: What job did many of Johann Sebastian Bach’s relatives have?
25541.e: The Bach family was a real family of musicians. Several of his sons also became well-known composers.
25541.m: There were many musicians in the Bach family.

25542.q: What happened to Beethoven’s hearing as he got older?
25542.e: Beethoven’s hearing got worse and worse until he was completely deaf. Even so, he carried on composing.
25542.m: Beethoven went deaf and still kept on composing.

25543.q: In which city did Beethoven live for most of his life?
25543.e: In 1792 Beethoven moved to Vienna. He stayed there until his death in 1827.
25543.m: Beethoven lived in Vienna for a long time.

25544.q: Which famous piano piece by Beethoven has a girl’s name in its title?
25544.e: “Für Elise” (For Elise) is one of the best-known piano pieces in the world. Many children learn it in piano lessons.
25544.m: “Für Elise” is a piano piece by Beethoven.

25545.q: On which instrument was Beethoven a great master?
25545.e: Beethoven was a brilliant pianist. In Vienna he thrilled people with his piano playing.

25546.q: How many symphonies did Beethoven write?
25546.e: Beethoven wrote 9 symphonies. The last one, the 9th Symphony, is especially famous.

25547.q: How could Beethoven compose even though he could no longer hear anything?
a: He heard the music in his head
25547.e: Beethoven knew the notes so well that he could imagine them in his head. So he wrote the music down without hearing it.
25547.m: Beethoven heard the music in his head.

25548.q: Which empire did Maria Theresa rule?
25548.e: From 1740 Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg lands, with Austria at their heart. She was one of the most powerful women of her time.

25549.q: How many children did Maria Theresa have?
25549.e: Maria Theresa had 16 children. Many of her daughters married kings and princes all over Europe.

25550.q: Which daughter of Maria Theresa became Queen of France?
25550.e: Marie Antoinette married the heir to the French throne in 1770. From 1774 she was Queen of France.
25550.m: Marie Antoinette was a daughter of Maria Theresa.

25551.q: Which palace in Vienna did Maria Theresa have extended as her summer residence?
25551.e: Maria Theresa had Schönbrunn Palace splendidly rebuilt. It is in Vienna and is a World Heritage Site today.
25551.m: Schönbrunn Palace was Maria Theresa’s favourite palace.

25552.q: What did Maria Theresa introduce for all children in 1774?
25552.e: In 1774 Maria Theresa introduced compulsory schooling for all. Children now had to go to school for at least six years.

25553.q: Which famous ruling family did Maria Theresa belong to?
25553.e: Maria Theresa was a Habsburg. The Habsburg family originally came from Aargau in Switzerland.
25553.m: Maria Theresa belonged to the Habsburg family.

25554.q: Which silver coin with Maria Theresa’s portrait was still being minted long after her death?
25554.e: The Maria Theresa thaler shows her portrait. It was so popular that it was still being minted long after her death.
25554.m: The Maria Theresa thaler shows Maria Theresa.

25555.q: What did the Montgolfier brothers invent?
25555.e: The brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier built the first hot-air balloon in 1783.
25555.m: The Montgolfier brothers invented the hot-air balloon.

25556.q: Which country did the Montgolfier brothers come from?
25556.e: The Montgolfier brothers came from Annonay in France. That is where they launched their first balloon.

25557.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
a: Warm air is lighter than cold air
25557.e: Warm air is lighter than the cold air outside. That is why the balloon full of hot air rises.

25558.q: Which animals were the first passengers in a hot-air balloon in 1783?
a: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel
A dog, a cat and a mouse
A horse, a cow and a goat
A monkey, a hare and a goose
25558.e: At Versailles a sheep, a duck and a cockerel flew in the basket. All three survived the short flight.
25558.m: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel were the first to fly in a balloon.

25559.q: In which year did the Montgolfier brothers’ first hot-air balloons go up?
25559.e: In 1783 the brothers launched their balloons in public. In the same year the first people flew too.
25559.m: The hot-air balloon first flew in 1783.

25560.q: How did the Montgolfier family earn their money?
25560.e: The family owned a paper factory. That is why the brothers built their balloons from cloth and paper.

25561.q: Over which city did people fly in a hot-air balloon for the first time in November 1783?
25561.e: On 21 November 1783 two men flew over Paris. They were in the air for about 25 minutes.
25561.m: The first people flew over Paris in 1783.

25562.q: Which prison in Paris did the people storm at the beginning of the Revolution?
25562.e: In summer 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille. It was a symbol of the King’s power.

25563.q: On which day does France celebrate its national holiday today?
25563.e: The holiday commemorates the start of the Revolution in 1789. On this day there are parades and fireworks in France.

25565.q: What colours is the flag that has stood for France since the Revolution?
25565.e: The French flag has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red. It is called the Tricolore.
25565.m: The French flag is blue, white and red.

25566.q: What is the French national anthem that was written during the Revolution called?
25566.e: La Marseillaise was written in 1792. Soldiers from Marseille sang it in Paris, which is where the name comes from.
25566.m: La Marseillaise is the anthem of France.

25568.q: Which country did Peter the Great rule?
25568.e: Peter the Great ruled Russia from 1682. He wanted to make his country more modern.

25569.q: What title did Russian rulers such as Peter the Great have?
25569.e: The rulers of Russia were called tsars. Peter later also took the title of emperor.
25569.m: Peter the Great was a Russian tsar.

25570.q: Which craft did Peter the Great learn on a journey to Holland?
25570.e: In disguise, Peter worked in a shipyard in Holland. He wanted to learn how to build good ships.
25570.m: Peter the Great learned shipbuilding in Holland.

25571.q: Under Peter the Great, what did Russian men have to pay if they wanted to keep a beard?
25571.e: Peter wanted Russians to look like Western Europeans. Anyone who wanted to keep his beard had to pay a beard tax.
25571.m: There was a beard tax under Peter the Great.

25572.q: Roughly how tall was Peter the Great?
25572.e: Peter was about 2 metres tall. So he really was a great big man.
25572.m: Peter the Great was about two metres tall.

25573.q: Which city on the Baltic Sea did Peter the Great found?
25573.e: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg on the Baltic Sea in 1703. The city became Russia’s new capital.
25573.m: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg.

25574.q: Which city did Peter the Great found?
25574.e: Peter the Great had the city built at the mouth of a river. It bears the name of his patron saint, Peter.
25574.m: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg.

25575.q: In which year was St Petersburg founded?
25575.e: St Petersburg was founded on 27 May 1703. First a fortress was built on an island.

25576.q: On which sea is St Petersburg?
25576.e: St Petersburg is on the Baltic Sea. Peter wanted a port so that Russia could trade with Western Europe.
25576.m: St Petersburg is on the Baltic Sea.

25577.q: In which country is the city of St Petersburg?
25577.e: St Petersburg is Russia’s second-largest city after Moscow. It lies in the north, by the sea.

25578.q: What role did St Petersburg have for about 200 years?
25578.e: Peter made St Petersburg the capital in 1712. Only in 1918 did Moscow become the capital again.
25578.m: St Petersburg was the capital of Russia for a long time.

25579.q: Because of its many canals, what is St Petersburg often called?
25579.e: Many canals with hundreds of bridges run through St Petersburg. That is why the city is compared with Venice.
25579.m: St Petersburg is also called the Venice of the North.

25580.q: Which country did Benjamin Franklin come from?
25580.e: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706. He was one of the founders of the United States of America.

25581.q: What did Benjamin Franklin fly in a thunderstorm to study lightning?
25581.e: According to tradition, Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm in 1752. That was very dangerous; never try anything like it!
25581.m: Franklin studied lightning with a kite.

25582.e: Benjamin Franklin’s face is on the American 100-dollar note. But he was never president.

25583.q: Which special kind of glasses is Benjamin Franklin said to have invented?
25583.e: Franklin split the lenses of his glasses into two halves. With the top part he could see into the distance, with the bottom part close up.
25583.m: Franklin had glasses for near and far.

25584.q: Which invention by Benjamin Franklin protects houses during thunderstorms?
25584.e: Franklin invented the lightning conductor around 1752. It stops lightning from setting houses on fire.
25584.m: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning conductor.

25585.q: Where does a lightning conductor send the lightning?
25585.e: The lightning conductor catches the lightning and carries it safely into the ground through a wire. That way the house is not damaged.
25585.m: The lightning conductor sends lightning into the ground.

25586.q: What material is a lightning conductor made of?
25586.e: A lightning conductor is made of metal such as copper or iron. Metal conducts electricity very well.
25586.m: A lightning conductor is made of metal.

25587.q: Where is a lightning conductor fitted?
a: In the garden under a tree
25587.e: The lightning conductor sits at the highest point of the house. That is where lightning is most likely to strike.
25587.m: The lightning conductor sits on top of the roof.

25588.q: What is lightning, as Benjamin Franklin found out?
25588.e: Franklin showed that lightning is a huge electrical discharge. That was an important discovery.

25590.q: On which day does the USA celebrate its Independence Day?
25590.e: 4 July is Independence Day in the USA. On this day there are fireworks and parades everywhere.
25590.m: The USA celebrates its birthday on 4 July.

25591.q: From which country did the American colonies want to become independent in 1776?
25591.e: The colonies belonged to Great Britain. They no longer wanted to be ruled by the British king.
25591.m: The USA broke away from Great Britain.

25592.q: Who became the first President of the USA?
25592.e: George Washington was first the leader of the army. In 1789 he became the first President of the USA.
25592.m: George Washington was the first President of the USA.

25593.q: How many colonies declared themselves independent in 1776?
25593.e: There were 13 colonies on the east coast. The 13 stripes on the US flag are a reminder of them.

25594.q: What did angry settlers throw into the sea at the “Boston Tea Party” in 1773?
25594.e: The settlers were against a tax on tea. So they threw whole chests of tea into the water in Boston harbour.
25594.m: At the Boston Tea Party, tea ended up in the sea.

25595.q: In which city was the Declaration of Independence signed?
25595.e: The representatives of the colonies met in Philadelphia. The famous Liberty Bell is there too.
25595.m: The Declaration of Independence was signed in Philadelphia.

25596.q: Which symbol did Louis XIV choose for himself?
25596.e: Louis XIV wanted to be at the centre like the Sun, with everything revolving around him. That is why you often see golden suns on his buildings.
25596.m: Louis XIV chose the Sun as his symbol.

25597.q: What is the period of Louis XIV called in art and architecture?
25597.e: In the time of Louis XIV, people built and painted in the Baroque style. Lots of gold, decoration and splendour are typical.
25597.m: Louis XIV lived in the Baroque period.

25598.q: Roughly how many rooms does the Palace of Versailles have?
25598.e: The Palace of Versailles has around 2,300 rooms. It is so big that you can get lost in it.
25598.m: The Palace of Versailles has over 2,000 rooms.

25599.q: What is there in the park at Versailles that you can go boating on?
25599.e: In the park is the Grand Canal, which is over a kilometre long. In the past, small ships even sailed there for the King.
25599.m: There is a long canal in the park at Versailles.

25600.q: What kind of hat did Napoleon usually wear?
25600.e: Napoleon wore a bicorne, a hat with two points. He often wore it sideways on his head.

25601.q: Which large gateway in Paris did Napoleon have built for his victories?
25601.e: Napoleon ordered the building of the Arc de Triomphe in 1806. It was meant to commemorate his army’s victories.
25601.m: The Arc de Triomphe in Paris commemorates Napoleon’s victories.

25602.q: What nickname did the soldiers give Napoleon?
25602.e: The soldiers fondly called Napoleon “the Little Corporal”. A corporal is a low rank in the army.
25602.m: The soldiers called Napoleon the Little Corporal.

25603.q: What were wigs often made from in the 18th century?
25603.e: Wigs were made by a special craftsman, the wigmaker. He used real human hair or animal hair, for example from horses or goats.
25603.m: Wigs were made from human or animal hair.

25604.q: Why did ladies in hoop skirts sometimes have to go through a door sideways?
a: The skirt was wider than the door
25604.e: Some hoop skirts were so wide that ladies had to go through doors sideways. That was very impractical.
25604.m: Wide hoop skirts hardly fitted through doors.

25605.q: Which trade did Benjamin Franklin learn as a young man?
25605.e: Franklin learned printing from his brother. Later he owned a printing shop and a newspaper himself.

25606.q: Which country did Benjamin Franklin travel to in order to get help for the fight for independence?
25606.e: From 1776 Franklin lived in France for several years. He persuaded the French king to help the Americans.
25606.m: Franklin got help for America in France.

25607.q: What did Benjamin Franklin found so that people could borrow books?
25607.e: In 1731 Franklin and his friends founded a lending library. He thought reading and learning were very important.

25608.q: How did the Montgolfier brothers heat the air in their balloon?
25608.e: A fire burned under the opening of the balloon, for example of straw and wool. The hot air filled the balloon.
25608.m: A fire heated the air in the balloon.

25609.q: Which king watched at Versailles in 1783 as a hot-air balloon carrying animals went up?
25609.e: King Louis XVI and his court watched the balloon launch at Versailles. Many spectators were amazed.
25609.m: Louis XVI saw one of the first balloon flights.

25610.q: What is a hot-air balloon also called, after its inventors?
25610.e: The Montgolfier brothers gave the hot-air balloon their name. That is why it is also called a montgolfière.
25610.m: A hot-air balloon is also called a montgolfière.

25611.q: What did Peter the Great build up for Russia so that it would be strong at sea?
25611.e: Peter had many ships built and founded the Russian navy. This made Russia much more powerful at sea.
25611.m: Peter the Great built up a Russian navy.

25612.q: What nickname does St Petersburg have because of its many canals?
25612.e: St Petersburg has many canals and hundreds of bridges. That is why it is called the Venice of the North.
25612.m: St Petersburg is also called the Venice of the North.

25613.q: How old was Maria Theresa when she became ruler in 1740?
25613.e: Maria Theresa was born in 1717 and took power in 1740. So she was only 23.

25614.q: What do the 50 stars on the US flag stand for today?
25614.e: Each star stands for one state of the USA. Today there are 50 states.
25614.m: The stars on the US flag stand for the states.

25615.q: Who improved the steam engine so that it worked much better?
25615.e: James Watt improved the steam engine from 1769 onwards. After that it needed much less fuel.
25615.m: James Watt made the steam engine much better.

25616.q: Which country did James Watt come from?
25616.e: James Watt was born in Greenock in Scotland in 1736. Scotland is part of Great Britain.

25617.e: Water is heated very strongly and turns into steam. The steam pushes a piston back and forth.
25617.m: A steam engine works with the power of steam.

25618.q: Where is the steam produced in a steam engine?
25618.e: A fire burns under the boiler. The water in the boiler boils and turns into steam.
25618.m: The steam is produced in the boiler.

25619.q: What were the first steam engines used for in mines?
25619.e: Water collected in deep pits. As early as 1712, steam engines pumped this water up to the surface.
25619.m: The first steam engines pumped water out of mines.

25620.q: Before the steam engine, where did factories often have to be?
a: In the middle of a forest
25620.e: Before that, machines were usually driven by a water wheel. With the steam engine, factories could be built almost anywhere.
25620.m: Without a steam engine, a factory needed a water wheel on a river.

25621.q: Before the steam engine, who turned the heavy wheels in many workshops?
25621.e: Before that, people or animals turned the wheels. The steam engine worked harder and without a break.
25621.m: The steam engine took heavy work off people and animals.

25622.q: What did James Watt compare the power of his engines with?
25622.e: Watt worked out how many horses an engine could replace. This is how horsepower came about.
25622.m: Horsepower compares an engine with horses.

25623.q: What is the wagon directly behind a steam locomotive that carries coal and water called?
25623.e: The tender held the supplies for the whole journey. Without them, the engine would soon have come to a stop.
25623.m: The tender carries the steam locomotive’s supplies.

25624.q: Which country did the locomotive builder George Stephenson come from?
25624.e: George Stephenson was born in Wylam near Newcastle in 1781. There were many coal mines there.

25626.q: Which places did the Spanish-Brötli Railway connect?
25626.e: The Spanish-Brötli Railway ran from Zurich to Baden in Aargau. It got its name from a tasty pastry from Baden, the “Spanisch Brötli”.
25626.m: The Spanish-Brötli Railway ran from Zurich to Baden.

25627.q: Who shovelled the coal into the fire on a steam locomotive?
25627.e: The fireman kept a strong fire going under the boiler. The engine driver drove the locomotive.
25627.m: The fireman kept the steam locomotive’s fire going.

25628.q: What came out of the chimney of a steam locomotive?
25628.e: Coal burned in the fire, which made smoke. On top of that came steam from the boiler.
25628.m: Smoke and steam came out of the steam locomotive’s chimney.

25629.q: What was one of Switzerland’s first locomotives called, named after a river in Zurich?
25629.e: The locomotive “Limmat” ran on the first railway line between Zurich and Baden. A replica is now in the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.
25629.m: The Limmat was one of Switzerland’s first locomotives.

25630.q: Where in Lucerne can you see old locomotives and steamboats?
a: At the Swiss Museum of Transport
25630.e: The Swiss Museum of Transport shows vehicles on land, on water and in the air. It is one of the most visited museums in Switzerland.
25630.m: At the Museum of Transport in Lucerne you can see old vehicles.

25631.q: What do you make with a loom?
25631.e: On a loom, threads are crossed over each other. This makes cloth for clothes and towels.
25631.m: A loom is used to make cloth.

25632.q: What do you call a factory where cloth is woven?
25632.e: In a weaving mill, many looms stand in large halls. It was very noisy there.
25632.m: Cloth is woven in a weaving mill.

25633.q: What happened in Uster in the canton of Zurich in 1832?
a: Workers set fire to a factory
25633.e: Many hand weavers were afraid that machines would take away their work. So they burned down a factory. This is called the Uster fire.
25633.m: In the Uster fire, weavers fought back against the machines.

25634.q: Which material did many Swiss factories process in the 19th century?
25634.e: There were many textile factories, especially in eastern Switzerland and the Zurich Oberland. They mainly processed cotton.
25634.m: Cotton was very important in Swiss factories.

25635.q: What was used to control Joseph-Marie Jacquard’s loom?
25635.e: The holes in the cards determined the pattern in the cloth. This allowed the machine to weave beautiful patterns.
25635.m: Jacquard’s loom read patterns from punched cards.

25636.q: Where did many people weave before there were factories?
25636.e: Many families had a loom in their living room. This is called home working.
25636.m: Before factories, many people wove at home.

25637.q: What are the two kinds of thread in weaving called?
25637.e: The warp threads are stretched out lengthwise. The weft thread runs across through them.
25637.m: In weaving, warp and weft cross each other.

25638.q: How long did children often work in factories in one day?
25638.e: Children often worked 12 hours or even longer. There was hardly any time left for playing.
25638.m: Factory children had to work very long hours.

25639.q: Why did many children have to work in the past?
a: They wanted to get to know machines
25639.e: The parents’ wages were often not enough to live on. So every child had to earn some money.
25639.m: Many children worked because their families were poor.

25640.q: Why did children have to crawl under the spinning machines?
a: Because they were quick at maths
25640.e: Under the machines, children picked up fibres or tied threads. That was very dangerous.
25640.m: Small children did dangerous work under the machines.

25641.q: What did children get for their work in the factory?
25641.e: Children earned much less than adults. That is why factory owners liked to employ children.

25642.q: What work did many poor boys from Ticino once do in foreign cities?
25642.e: The boys were small and fitted into narrow chimneys. Many went to Milan, for example.
25642.m: Chimney-sweep children from Ticino had a hard life.

25643.q: What did children often have to do in coal mines?
25643.e: In narrow passages, children pulled or pushed heavy carts. Others opened doors for the air.
25643.m: Children had to do hard work in mines too.

25644.q: Are children allowed to work in factories in Switzerland today?
25644.e: Today laws protect children in Switzerland. Children go to school instead of to the factory.
25644.m: Today factory work for children is forbidden in Switzerland.

25645.q: Since when has the Federal Constitution required all cantons to have compulsory schooling?
25645.e: The Federal Constitution of 1874 required a primary school for all children. Before that, it was different in every canton.
25645.m: Since 1874 all children in Switzerland have had to go to school.

25646.q: How much does it cost to attend a state school in Switzerland?
25646.e: State schools are free of charge. This means all children can learn, no matter how much money their parents have.
25646.m: State school in Switzerland is free.

25647.q: Who is mainly responsible for schools in Switzerland?
25647.e: Each canton has its own school laws. That is why schools are not the same everywhere.
25647.m: The cantons decide about their schools.

25648.q: Which school do children in Switzerland go to after kindergarten?
25648.e: After kindergarten, primary school begins. There you learn reading, writing and maths.

25649.q: Why did compulsory schooling help against child labour?
a: Children had to be at school during the day
25649.e: Anyone sitting in school cannot work in a factory at the same time. So children had more time to learn.
25649.m: Compulsory schooling got children out of the factories.

25650.q: How many years does compulsory schooling last in most cantons today?
25650.e: Under the HarmoS agreement, it includes 2 years of kindergarten, 6 years of primary school and 3 years of lower secondary school (as of 2025). That makes 11 years altogether.

25651.q: What did schoolchildren often write on in the 19th century?
25651.e: Paper was expensive. So children wrote with a slate pencil on a small slate and wiped it clean again.
25651.m: Children used to write on slates.

25652.q: What do you call people who dig coal underground?
25652.e: Miners work deep underground in pits.
25652.m: Miners get coal out of the ground.

25653.q: Which bird warned miners about poisonous gas?
25653.e: The little bird noticed poisonous gas sooner than people did. If it became weak, the miners had to get out quickly.
25653.m: The canary was a warning sign in the mine.

25654.q: Which animals pulled the coal carts in many mines?
25654.e: Small horses, called pit ponies, pulled the carts through the passages. Some lived underground for a long time.

25655.e: A very long time ago, forests and swamps were buried under earth. Over millions of years this turned into coal.
25655.m: Coal formed from plants of long ago.

25656.q: What did Humphry Davy invent for miners around 1815?
25656.e: An open flame could make the gas in the mine explode. Davy’s lamp had a fine wire mesh around the flame.
25656.m: The safety lamp made mines safer.

25657.q: What is the name of a large coal-mining area in Germany?
25657.e: There were very many coal mines in the Ruhr. Large industrial cities grew up there.
25657.m: The Ruhr was an important coal-mining area.

25658.q: Where did Switzerland get most of its coal from in the 19th century?
25658.e: There was only a little poor-quality coal in Switzerland. So most of it came by train from neighbouring countries.

25659.q: What turned at the side of many old steamboats?
25659.e: The steam engine turned large wheels. Their paddles pushed the boat through the water.
25659.m: Paddle steamers are driven by paddle wheels.

25660.q: Who operated the steam engine on a steamboat?
25660.e: The engineer worked down in the engine room. He made sure the engine ran properly.
25660.m: The engineer looks after the ship’s engine.

25661.q: On which lake did Switzerland’s first steamboat sail in 1823?
25661.e: The boat was called the “Guillaume Tell”. It sailed between Geneva and other places on the lake.
25661.m: The first Swiss steamboat sailed on Lake Geneva.

25662.q: On which lake do the paddle steamers “Uri” and “Unterwalden” sail?
25662.e: Several old paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne. The “Uri” has been in service since 1901.
25662.m: Old paddle steamers still sail on Lake Lucerne.

25663.q: On which lake does the paddle steamer “Blüemlisalp” sail?
25663.e: The “Blüemlisalp” is named after a mountain range in the Bernese Oberland. It has been sailing on Lake Thun since 1906.
25663.m: The Blüemlisalp is a steamboat on Lake Thun.

25664.q: Which famous steamship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
25664.e: The Titanic was on its first voyage to America. More than 1,500 people died.
25664.m: The Titanic sank in the Atlantic in 1912.

25665.q: What was a big advantage of steamships over sailing ships?
25665.e: A sailing ship has to wait when there is no wind. A steamship can sail without wind and even against it.
25665.m: Steamships did not depend on the wind.

25666.q: What were the tall factory chimneys for?
25666.e: The smoke from the furnaces was meant to rise high up into the air. A tall chimney also draws better.
25666.m: The factory chimney carries the smoke upwards.

25667.q: What were many factory chimneys built from?
25667.e: Bricks can withstand great heat and do not burn. Many old red-brick chimneys are still standing today.
25667.m: Many factory chimneys are built of brick.

25668.q: What often formed in London from smoke and fog?
25668.e: The word smog is made from “smoke” and “fog”. Smog makes the air dirty.
25668.m: Smog is a mixture of smoke and fog.

25669.q: What settled on houses and washing because of the factory smoke?
25669.e: The smoke contained lots of black particles. They made walls and fresh washing dark.

25670.q: Which moth often became darker in smoky areas of England?
25670.e: On dark, sooty trees, birds could easily see the light moths. Dark moths survived better.
25670.m: The peppered moth adapted to the soot.

25671.q: What was burned in factories, producing dark smoke?
25671.e: Coal was the most important fuel of industrialisation. When it burns, it gives off a lot of smoke.
25671.m: Burning coal made the factory smoke.

25672.q: What effect did all the smoke have on people?
25672.e: The dirty air irritated the lungs. Many people in industrial towns became ill.

25673.q: How did working families in towns often live?
25673.e: Often a whole family lived in one or two rooms. Rents were high and wages were low.
25673.m: Working families often lived very crowded together.

25674.q: Where was the toilet in many workers’ houses?
a: In the yard, shared by everyone
In the cellar of each flat
25674.e: Many families shared a simple toilet in the yard or on the stairs. A bathroom of your own was rare.
25674.m: In the past, many families shared one toilet.

a: Someone who rented only a bed
A man who walked in his sleep
25675.e: Many families rented out a bed to earn money. The bed lodger was only allowed to sleep there.
25675.m: A bed lodger rented only a place to sleep.

25676.q: Which disease spread in towns through dirty water?
25676.e: Sewage got into the drinking water. That is how many people caught cholera.

25677.q: Why did some factory owners build houses for their workers?
a: So they lived close to the factory
So they could go on holiday
25677.e: This way the workers got to work quickly. Such housing is called a workers’ estate.
25677.m: Workers’ estates were often close to the factory.

25678.q: What are the large tenement blocks for workers in Berlin called?
25678.e: The buildings had many storeys and narrow back courtyards. Very many people lived in them.
25678.m: In Berlin many workers lived in Mietskasernen (rental barracks).

25679.q: Where did many working families get their water from?
a: From their own spring in the cellar
25679.e: Running water in the flat was rare. People carried water home in buckets.
25679.m: People often used to fetch water from the well.

25680.q: How much did Henry Ford pay many workers per day from 1914?
25680.e: At the time, that was about twice as much as in other factories. Ford wanted to keep good workers in his factory.
25680.m: From 1914 Ford paid five dollars a day.

25681.q: Which car did Henry Ford have built on the assembly line?
25681.e: The Model T was built from 1908 to 1927. It was one of the first cars for ordinary families.
25681.m: The Model T was Ford’s assembly-line car.

25682.q: What does a worker on an assembly line do?
a: The same step over and over
25682.e: Each worker had a small task, for example screwing on a wheel. It was fast, but monotonous.
25682.m: On the assembly line, everyone does a small part of the work.

25683.q: What happened to the price of cars because of the assembly line?
25683.e: The cars were finished much faster. That is why Ford could sell them more cheaply.
25683.m: The assembly line made cars cheaper.

25684.q: Near which city was Ford’s factory with the assembly line?
25684.e: The factory was in Highland Park near Detroit in the north of the USA. Detroit became the car city.
25684.m: Detroit is known as the car city.

25685.q: What colour were most Model T cars?
25685.e: Black paint dried quickly back then. That is why for many years the car only came in black.
25685.m: The Model T was mostly black.

25686.q: What moves along the assembly line in a car factory?
25686.e: The belt brings the car from one station to the next. The workers stay at their places.
25686.m: With an assembly line, the work comes to the worker.

25687.q: In which year was the Eiffel Tower finished?
25687.e: Building it took about two years. In spring 1889 the tower was finished.
25687.m: The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.

25688.q: What material is the Eiffel Tower made of?
25688.e: The tower is made of many thousands of wrought-iron parts. The metal is repainted regularly.
25688.m: The Eiffel Tower is an iron tower.

25689.q: Who is the Eiffel Tower named after?
25689.e: Gustave Eiffel was an engineer. His company built the tower.
25689.m: The Eiffel Tower bears Gustave Eiffel’s name.

25690.q: Roughly how tall was the Eiffel Tower when it opened?
25690.e: The tower was about 300 metres tall. For a long time it was the tallest structure in the world.
25690.m: The Eiffel Tower was about 300 metres tall.

25691.q: What was supposed to happen to the Eiffel Tower after about 20 years?
a: It was to be taken down
It was to be covered in gold
It was to be moved to London
It was to be built higher
25691.e: The tower was only planned to stand for a certain time. Because it was needed for radio aerials, it stayed.
25691.m: The Eiffel Tower was actually meant to disappear again.

25692.q: How were the iron parts of the Eiffel Tower joined together?
25692.e: Workers hammered red-hot rivets into the holes. As they cooled, they held the parts firmly together.
25692.m: Millions of rivets hold the Eiffel Tower together.

25693.q: How can you send Morse code even without electricity?
a: With a flag or flashes of light
25693.e: Morse code is made of short and long signals. You can send them with sounds, flashes of light or a flag.
25693.m: Morse code can also be sent with light.

25694.q: What is Morse code made up of?
25694.e: A dot is a short signal and a dash a long one. Together they make letters.
25694.m: Morse code has short and long signals.

25695.q: Which distress call is sent in Morse with three short, three long and three short signals?
25695.e: Three short signals are an S, three long ones an O. The distress call is easy to remember.
25695.m: SOS is the best-known distress call.

25696.q: How did a message travel with the electric telegraph?
25696.e: The electricity flowed through long cables in seconds. So the message arrived much faster than a letter.
25696.m: The telegraph sent messages through wires.

25697.q: What is a message sent by telegraph called?
25697.e: A telegram was short because every word cost money. A messenger brought it to your home.
25697.m: A telegram is a message sent by telegraph.

25698.q: What was successfully laid across the Atlantic in 1866?
25698.e: A long cable on the sea floor connected Europe and America. Messages now arrived in minutes instead of days.
25698.m: A cable under the sea connected Europe with America.

25699.q: Which letter is just a single dot in Morse code?
25699.e: E is the most common letter in English. That is why it got the shortest signal.
25699.m: In Morse code, E is just one dot.

25700.q: Where is the hole for the thread on a sewing machine needle?
25700.e: On a hand-sewing needle the eye is at the top. On a machine needle it is at the bottom, near the point.
25700.m: A sewing machine needle has its eye at the bottom.

25701.q: How many threads does a sewing machine need for a normal stitch?
25701.e: There is an upper thread and a lower thread. They loop around each other in the fabric.
25701.m: A sewing machine sews with two threads.

25702.q: How were many old sewing machines powered?
25702.e: You pushed a treadle with your feet. That left your hands free for the fabric.
25702.m: Old sewing machines were powered by foot.

25703.q: What is the small part that the lower thread is wound onto called?
25703.e: The bobbin sits in the machine underneath the needle. That is where the lower thread comes from.
25703.m: The lower thread is on a bobbin.

25704.q: What could be made much faster with sewing machines?
25704.e: By hand, a shirt took many hours. With the machine it was much faster.
25704.m: The sewing machine made sewing clothes faster.

25705.q: What was the sewing machine especially important for in the 19th century?
25705.e: With a sewing machine you could sew much faster than by hand. So clothes were made in large quantities in factories.
25705.m: The sewing machine made producing clothes much faster.

25706.q: What was the name of the American whose sewing machines became world-famous?
25706.e: Isaac Singer improved the sewing machine and sold it in large numbers from 1851. His company, Singer, became world-famous.
25706.m: Isaac Singer’s sewing machines became world-famous.

25707.q: In which city was the first World’s Fair held in 1851?
25707.e: The first World’s Fair, the Great Exhibition, was held in Hyde Park. Many countries showed their goods there.
25707.m: The first World’s Fair was in London.

25708.q: What was the large glass and iron building of the first World’s Fair called?
25708.e: The gardener Joseph Paxton designed the huge building. It looked like a giant greenhouse.
25708.m: The Crystal Palace was made of glass and iron.

25709.q: What did countries show at a World’s Fair?
25709.e: Countries wanted to show what new things they could do. Visitors marvelled at machines and inventions.
25709.m: World’s Fairs show new things from all over the world.

25710.q: Which attraction appeared for the first time in Chicago in 1893?
25710.e: George Ferris built the big wheel for the World’s Fair. It was about 80 metres tall.
25710.m: The first big Ferris wheel turned in Chicago in 1893.

25711.q: Which structure has stood in Brussels since the 1958 World’s Fair?
25711.e: The Atomium looks like a hugely enlarged iron crystal with nine spheres. Today it is a museum.
25711.m: The Atomium in Brussels comes from a World’s Fair.

25712.q: Which device did Alexander Graham Bell show at the 1876 World’s Fair in Philadelphia?
25712.e: Bell showed his new device for talking over a wire. Visitors could hear a voice from far away.
25712.m: Alexander Graham Bell showed the telephone.

25713.q: In which country was a World Expo held in 2025?
25713.e: Expo 2025 was held in Osaka. Switzerland also had a pavilion there.
25713.m: The 2025 World Expo was in Osaka in Japan.

25714.q: Which inventor made the light bulb famous?
25714.e: Thomas Edison and his team built a light bulb that shone for many hours. After that, electric light spread all over the world.
25714.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb well known.

25715.q: In which year did Edison present his long-lasting light bulb?
25715.e: Edison and his team presented their long-lasting light bulb in 1879. It shone for many hours.

25716.q: Which country did Thomas Edison come from?
25716.e: Thomas Edison was born in the US state of Ohio in 1847. He lived and worked mainly in the USA.
25716.m: Thomas Edison was an inventor from the USA.

25717.q: What glows inside an old light bulb and gives light?
25717.e: In a light bulb, electricity flows through a very thin filament. The filament gets hot, glows and gives light.
25717.m: In a light bulb, a hot, thin filament gives light.

25718.q: Before the light bulb, what did many people use for light in the evening?
25718.e: Before the electric light bulb there were candles, oil lamps and gas lamps. These lights had an open flame.
25718.m: In the past, candles and oil lamps burned in the evening.

25719.q: Roughly how many patents did Thomas Edison have?
25719.e: During his life, Thomas Edison registered over 1,000 inventions as patents. That is why he is seen as one of the hardest-working inventors.
25719.m: Thomas Edison had over a thousand patents.

25720.q: Which lamp mostly replaces the old light bulb today?
25720.e: LED lamps give lots of light and use only a little electricity. Old light bulbs, on the other hand, get very hot and waste energy.
25720.m: LED lamps save a lot of electricity.

25721.q: In which country was Bell living when he invented the telephone?
25721.e: Bell was living in Boston in the USA at the time. There he built the telephone with his assistant.
25721.m: Bell invented the telephone in the USA.

25722.q: In which year did Bell receive his patent for the telephone?
25722.e: The patent for Bell’s telephone dates from 1876. That is about 150 years ago.

25723.q: In which country was Alexander Graham Bell born?
25723.e: Bell was born in Edinburgh in 1847. Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.
25723.m: Alexander Graham Bell came from Scotland.

25724.q: What could be transmitted with the first telephone?
25724.e: The telephone turns the voice into electrical signals. At the other end they become sound again.
25724.m: With the telephone you can send your voice over long distances.

25725.q: Which people did Bell work with as a teacher?
25725.e: Bell taught deaf people and was very interested in speech and sound. This helped him invent the telephone.
25725.m: Bell was a teacher of deaf people.

25726.q: What was the name of Bell’s assistant, to whom he spoke the first sentence on the telephone?
25726.e: Bell called through the telephone to his assistant Thomas Watson, asking him to come over. Watson heard him in the other room.
25726.m: Bell’s assistant at the first telephone was called Watson.

25727.q: What did the German teacher Philipp Reis build as early as around 1861?
25727.e: Philipp Reis built a device that could transmit sounds. He was already calling it a “Telephon”.
25727.m: Philipp Reis built an early telephone in Germany.

25728.q: What were the first telephones connected with?
25728.e: Early telephones needed long wires between the devices. Mobile phones without cables came much later.
25728.m: The first telephones were connected by wires.

25729.q: Who built the first real car with a petrol engine?
25729.e: Carl Benz built a motor car and applied for a patent for it. This patent is seen as the car’s birth certificate.
25729.m: Carl Benz built the first car with a petrol engine.

25730.q: How many wheels did Carl Benz’s first motor car have?
25730.e: The Benz Patent Motor Car had two large wheels at the back and one at the front. It looked almost like a big tricycle.
25730.m: Benz’s first car had three wheels.

25731.q: In which year did Carl Benz apply for a patent for his car?
25731.e: On 29 January 1886 Carl Benz registered his motor car at the patent office. That is why 1886 is seen as the year the car was born.

25732.q: In which German city did Carl Benz build his first car?
25732.e: Carl Benz had his workshop in Mannheim. There he built and tested his motor car.
25732.m: The first Benz car was made in Mannheim.

25733.q: How fast did Carl Benz’s first car go?
a: About as fast as a bike
As fast as a racing car
As fast as an express train
25733.e: The motor car went at most about 16 kilometres per hour. A cyclist is often just as fast.
25733.m: The first car was only as fast as a bike.

25734.q: Before the car was invented, what usually pulled carts and carriages?
25734.e: Before the car, coaches and carts were usually pulled by horses. That is why the car was first also called a “horseless carriage”.
25734.m: Before the car, horses pulled the carriages.

25735.q: Which other German inventor built a car at almost the same time as Benz?
25735.e: In the same year as Benz, Gottlieb Daimler built a carriage with an engine and four wheels. Later the companies of Benz and Daimler merged.
25735.m: Gottlieb Daimler also built an early car.

25736.q: How did you steer Carl Benz’s first car?
25736.e: The Patent Motor Car did not yet have a round steering wheel. You steered the front wheel with a crank handle.
25736.m: The first car was steered with a crank handle.

25737.e: Bertha Benz was married to Carl Benz. With her money and her courage, she helped make the car well known.
25737.m: Bertha Benz was Carl Benz’s wife.

25738.q: In which year did Bertha Benz make her famous long car journey?
25738.e: In August 1888 Bertha Benz secretly set off in the motor car. It was the first long journey by car.

25739.q: Where did Bertha Benz drive to on her famous journey?
25739.e: Bertha Benz drove to her home town of Pforzheim. Her mother lived there.

25740.q: Who went with Bertha Benz on her journey?
25740.e: Bertha Benz took her sons Eugen and Richard with her. Her husband Carl knew nothing about the trip.
25740.m: Bertha Benz travelled with her two sons.

25741.q: Roughly how long was Bertha Benz’s outward journey?
25741.e: The outward journey was about 106 kilometres long. For a car of those days, that was a huge trip.
25741.m: Bertha Benz drove more than a hundred kilometres.

25742.q: Where did Bertha Benz buy fuel on the way?
25742.e: There were no petrol stations yet. Bertha Benz bought the fuel at a chemist’s in Wiesloch.
25742.m: The first petrol station was a chemist’s.

25743.q: What did Bertha Benz use on the way to clean a blocked fuel line?
25743.e: Bertha Benz fixed many things herself on the way. She cleaned a blocked line with the long pin from her hat.
25743.m: Bertha Benz made do with a hatpin on the way.

25744.q: What did Bertha Benz use on the way to improve the brakes?
25744.e: On the way, Bertha Benz had leather fitted to the brakes. The car braked better, and that is why she is seen as the inventor of the brake lining.
25744.m: Bertha Benz improved the brakes with leather.

25745.q: Who invented the running machine, the forerunner of the bicycle?
25745.e: Karl Drais presented his running machine when there were no bicycles yet. It is seen as the ancestor of the bicycle.
25745.m: Karl Drais invented the running machine.

25746.q: In which year did Karl Drais first ride his running machine?
25746.e: On 12 June 1817 Karl Drais rode a longer distance on his running machine for the first time. That was the birth of the two-wheeler.
25746.m: The running machine was first ridden in 1817.

25747.q: How did you move the running machine forward?
a: With your feet on the ground
25747.e: You sat on the running machine and pushed yourself off the ground with your feet. That made it roll forward.
25747.m: On the running machine you pushed off with your feet.

25748.q: What material was the running machine mainly made of?
25748.e: The frame and wheels of the running machine were made of wood. Only a few parts were iron.
25748.m: The running machine was mostly made of wood.

25749.q: In which city was Karl Drais born?
25749.e: Karl Drais was born in Karlsruhe in 1785. The city is in south-west Germany.

25750.q: Which vehicle for small children works like the running machine today?
25750.e: On a balance bike, small children learn to keep their balance. It works exactly like Drais’s running machine.
25750.m: A balance bike works like Drais’s running machine.

25751.q: What is the running machine also called, after its inventor?
25751.e: After Karl Drais, the running machine was also called a draisine. Today small rail vehicles are called that too.
25751.m: The running machine is also called a draisine.

25752.q: What did the running machine still lack that a bicycle has today?
25752.e: The running machine already had a saddle and handlebars, but no pedals yet. Pedals were only added a few decades later.
25752.m: The running machine had no pedals yet.

25753.q: How long did the very first surviving photograph, from around 1826, need to be exposed?
25753.e: The first light-sensitive plates reacted to light only very slowly. That is why the camera had to stay pointed at the same scene for hours.
25753.m: The first photos needed exposures lasting hours.

25754.q: What does the oldest surviving photograph in the world show?
25754.e: Niépce pointed his camera out of an upstairs window of his country house. You can see roofs and buildings.
25754.m: The oldest photo shows the view from a window.

25755.q: Roughly how long did it take to take the first photograph?
25755.e: The plate had to lie in the light for many hours, perhaps even days. Today a mobile phone takes a photo in a fraction of a second.
25755.m: The first photograph took many hours.

25756.q: Which country did Nicéphore Niépce come from?
25756.e: Nicéphore Niépce was a French inventor. He lived in a village in Burgundy.

25757.q: What were the pictures made on in the daguerreotype process?
25757.e: Louis Daguerre developed a process for sharp pictures on silver-coated metal plates. It was named the daguerreotype after him.
25757.m: Daguerreotypes are pictures on silver-coated plates.

25758.q: In which year was the daguerreotype presented to the public?
25758.e: In 1839 Daguerre’s process was made public in Paris. That is why 1839 is often seen as the year photography was born.

25759.q: What colours did the first photographs have?
25759.e: The first photographs were black and white or brownish. Colour photos only came much later.
25759.m: The first photos were not in colour.

25760.q: Why did people have to sit still for a long time for early photos?
a: Otherwise the picture would be blurred
Otherwise the picture would be colourful
25760.e: Early cameras took a long time to finish the picture. Anyone who moved came out blurred in the photo.
25760.m: For early photos you had to keep still for a long time.

25761.q: What are the Lumière brothers famous for?
a: They were the first to show films to a paying audience.
25761.e: Auguste and Louis Lumière built a camera that could record and project films. In 1895 they showed films to a paying audience in Paris.
25761.m: The Lumière brothers were among the inventors of cinema.

25762.q: Which country did the Lumière brothers come from?
25762.e: The Lumière brothers lived and worked in Lyon in France. Their father had a factory there for photographic plates.
25762.m: The Lumière brothers came from France.

25763.q: In which city did the Lumière brothers first show films to a paying audience?
25763.e: They showed their films in a room underneath a café in Paris. The audience paid for entry.
25763.m: The Lumières’ first cinema screening was in Paris.

25764.q: In which year is cinema said to have been born?
25764.e: The Lumière brothers’ screening for a paying audience in December 1895 is seen as the birth of cinema.

25765.q: What came towards the audience in one of the very first films?
25765.e: The Lumière brothers’ film shows a train pulling into a station. People say that some viewers got a fright.
25765.m: A famous early film shows a train arriving.

25766.q: Roughly how long were the Lumières’ first films?
25766.e: The first films were very short and did not even last a minute. No more film would fit in the camera.
25766.m: The first films were shorter than a minute.

25767.q: What did the Lumières’ first films still lack?
25767.e: The first films were silent films without sound. Sometimes someone in the hall played the piano along with them.
25767.m: The first films were silent films.

25768.q: What was the Lumières’ device that could both film and show films called?
25768.e: The Lumière brothers’ cinematograph could record films and project them onto a wall. The word cinema comes from the word cinematograph.
25768.m: The word cinema comes from the cinematograph.

25769.e: Emil Berliner applied for a patent for the gramophone in 1887. He was born in Germany and lived in the USA.

25770.q: What do you play on a gramophone?
25770.e: A record turns on the gramophone. Music is stored on it.

25771.e: A record is a round, flat disc. The music is in fine grooves.
25771.m: A record is a round disc.

25772.q: On a gramophone, what runs through the grooves of the record?
25772.e: A fine needle glides through the grooves of the record. It vibrates as it goes, and that makes the sound.
25772.m: On a gramophone, a needle reads the grooves.

25773.q: Which large part made the music louder on an old gramophone?
25773.e: Old gramophones had a large horn. It made the quiet sound from the needle louder.
25773.m: The horn made the gramophone’s music louder.

25774.q: How did you get an old gramophone going?
25774.e: You turned a crank and wound up a spring with it. The spring then turned the turntable.
25774.m: Old gramophones were wound up with a crank.

25775.q: Which sound device did Thomas Edison invent as early as 1877?
25775.e: With Edison’s phonograph, sounds could be recorded and played back for the first time. The first thing Edison spoke into it was a nursery rhyme.

25776.q: What did Edison’s phonograph record sounds on?
25776.e: The phonograph stored sounds on a cylinder that looks like a roll. Berliner used flat discs instead.
25776.m: The phonograph recorded sounds on a cylinder.

25777.q: Which Italian was one of the first to send messages through the air without wires?
25777.e: From 1895 Guglielmo Marconi experimented with wireless radio. He is seen as a pioneer of radio.
25777.m: Guglielmo Marconi was a pioneer of wireless.

25778.q: What does a radio need to receive programmes?
25778.e: Radio stations send invisible radio waves through the air. The aerial picks up these waves.
25778.m: A radio picks up radio waves with an aerial.

25779.q: What can you do with a radio?
25779.e: A radio receives sounds from a station. You can listen to music, news and stories.
25779.m: With a radio you listen to music and news.

25780.q: What was the name of the national transmitter that broadcast radio for German-speaking Switzerland from 1931?
25780.e: The Beromünster national transmitter in the canton of Lucerne broadcast from 1931. For decades it was the most important station in German-speaking Switzerland.
25780.m: Beromünster was the radio station of German-speaking Switzerland.

25781.q: Which prize did the radio inventor Guglielmo Marconi receive in 1909?
25781.e: Marconi developed wireless transmission with radio waves. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909, together with Ferdinand Braun.
25781.m: Marconi received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

25782.q: What did the Titanic’s radio operator send in 1912 as the ship sank?
25782.e: As the Titanic sank, the radio operator sent distress calls. Another ship came and rescued many people.
25782.m: The Titanic sent distress calls by radio in 1912.

25784.q: What were the Wright brothers’ first names?
25784.e: Orville and Wilbur Wright were brothers from the USA. They built the first powered aeroplane that could fly under control.
25784.m: The Wright brothers were called Orville and Wilbur.

25785.q: In which year did the Wright brothers first fly with an engine?
25785.e: On 17 December 1903, the first controlled powered flight succeeded near Kitty Hawk in the USA. The aeroplane was heavier than air.

25786.q: How long did the Wright brothers’ first flight last?
25786.e: The first flight lasted only about 12 seconds. Even so, it was a huge success.
25786.m: The first powered flight lasted only 12 seconds.

25787.q: Roughly how far did the aeroplane fly on the Wrights’ very first flight?
25787.e: On the first flight, the Flyer covered about 37 metres. That is shorter than a football pitch.
25787.m: The first flight was shorter than a football pitch.

25788.q: What business did the Wright brothers have before they built aeroplanes?
25788.e: The Wright brothers sold and repaired bicycles in Dayton. With the money they paid for their flying experiments.
25788.m: The Wright brothers had a bicycle shop.

25789.q: What was the Wright brothers’ first powered aeroplane called?
25789.e: The Wright brothers’ aeroplane was called the Flyer. It had two wings, one above the other, and a small engine.
25789.m: The Wrights’ first aeroplane was called the Flyer.

25790.q: Which of the two brothers was at the controls on the first successful flight?
25790.e: On the first successful flight, Orville Wright lay on the aeroplane and steered. Wilbur ran alongside.
25790.m: Orville Wright steered the first powered flight.

25791.q: Which German flew gliders even before the Wrights?
25791.e: From 1891 Otto Lilienthal flew home-made gliders without an engine. The Wright brothers learned a lot from him.
25791.m: Otto Lilienthal flew gliders before the Wrights.

25792.e: A zeppelin is a huge airship with a rigid frame. It floats because it is filled with gas.
25792.m: A zeppelin is a large airship.

25793.q: Why could a zeppelin float in the air?
a: It was filled with a light gas
It was made of very thin paper
25793.e: Inside a zeppelin’s envelope was a gas that is lighter than air. That is why the airship floated upwards.
25793.m: A zeppelin floats thanks to a light gas.

25794.q: Over which lake did the first zeppelin fly?
25794.e: The first airship, LZ 1, rose over Lake Constance. Lake Constance also borders Switzerland.
25794.m: The first zeppelin flew over Lake Constance.

25795.q: In which year did the first zeppelin fly?
25795.e: On 2 July 1900 the airship LZ 1 flew for the first time. It was in the air even before the first powered aeroplane.

25796.q: Which gas were the old zeppelins filled with?
25796.e: The old zeppelins were filled with hydrogen. This gas is very light, but it can catch fire easily.

25797.q: What was the name of the famous zeppelin that burned in the USA in 1937?
25797.e: The airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing in Lakehurst in 1937. After that, the era of the great passenger zeppelins ended.

25798.q: In which German town were many zeppelins built?
25798.e: The large hangars of the Zeppelin works stood in Friedrichshafen on Lake Constance. Today there is a Zeppelin Museum there.
25798.m: Many zeppelins were built in Friedrichshafen.

25799.q: In which year did a first trial television programme begin in Switzerland?
25799.e: In 1953 the SRG broadcast a first trial programme in Zurich. It only ran for about an hour in the evening.
25799.m: Swiss television began with trials in 1953.

25800.q: Which organisation has made radio and television for all parts of Switzerland since the beginning?
25800.e: The SRG broadcasts programmes in German, French, Italian and Romansh. It also started Swiss television in the 1950s.
25800.m: The SRG makes radio and television in Switzerland.

25801.q: What colours were the pictures on the first televisions?
25801.e: The first televisions only showed black, white and shades of grey. Colour television came later.
25801.m: The first televisions showed black-and-white pictures.

25802.q: In which year did colour television come to Switzerland?
25802.e: In 1968 Swiss television began broadcasting in colour. At first there were only a few colour programmes.
25802.m: Switzerland has had colour television since 1968.

25803.q: What did the pictures on the first television sets look like?
a: black and white and rather blurry
25803.e: The first television pictures were small, blurry and black and white. Colour television only came much later.
25803.m: Early television was black and white.

25804.q: What does a television transmit in addition, compared with radio?
25804.e: Radio only transmits sounds. Television also shows moving pictures.
