25805.q: Where did ETH Zurich show Switzerland’s first television experiment in 1939?
25805.e: At the 1939 National Exhibition in Zurich, ETH showed a television experiment. Visitors were amazed by the pictures.
25805.m: The first Swiss television experiment was at the 1939 National Exhibition (Landi).

25806.q: How did people keep food cool before there were fridges?
25806.e: In the past, food was stored in cool cellars. In winter, people sawed ice from lakes and kept it.
25806.m: Before the fridge, people kept things cool with ice and cellars.

25807.q: Which German engineer built an important refrigerating machine around 1876?
25807.e: In the 1870s Carl von Linde developed a refrigerating machine that used ammonia. It was an important basis for later fridges.
25807.m: Carl von Linde built an important refrigerating machine.

25808.q: Where were Linde’s first refrigerating machines mainly used?
25808.e: Breweries needed a lot of cooling to make beer. That is why they were the first to buy Linde’s machines.
25808.m: Linde’s refrigerating machines first cooled breweries.

25809.q: Why do we put milk in the fridge?
a: So there is more of it
25809.e: In the cold, bacteria multiply more slowly. So the milk does not go off as quickly.
25809.m: Food stays fresh longer in the fridge.

25810.q: Which famous physicist invented a fridge together with Leo Szilard?
25810.e: Around 1930 Albert Einstein and Leo Szilard patented a fridge with no moving parts. Einstein had earlier worked at the patent office in Bern.
25810.m: Albert Einstein also invented a fridge.

25811.q: Roughly when did many families in Switzerland get a fridge?
25811.e: After the Second World War, fridges became cheaper. In the 1950s and 1960s they appeared in more and more Swiss kitchens.
25811.m: Fridges came into many kitchens in the 1950s and 1960s.

25812.q: What does a modern fridge need in order to keep things cool?
25812.e: A modern fridge has a compressor that runs on electricity. Without electricity, it slowly gets warm inside.
25812.m: A fridge needs electricity to keep cool.

25813.q: In which country was Marie Curie born?
25813.e: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867. Warsaw is the capital of Poland.

25814.q: In which city did Marie Curie do research for most of her life?
25814.e: As a young woman, Marie Curie moved to Paris to study there. Afterwards she stayed in Paris and did her research there.
25814.m: Marie Curie did her research in Paris.

25815.q: How many Nobel Prizes did Marie Curie receive?
25815.e: She received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.
25815.m: Marie Curie received two Nobel Prizes.

25816.q: Which element did Marie Curie discover?
25816.e: In 1898 Marie Curie and her husband Pierre discovered radium. Radium glows faintly in the dark.

25817.q: Which country did Marie Curie name the element polonium after?
25817.e: Marie Curie wanted to honour her homeland. That is why she named the new element polonium, after Poland.

25818.q: What was the name of Marie Curie’s husband, with whom she did research?
25818.e: Marie and Pierre Curie worked together in the laboratory. In 1903 they received the Nobel Prize together.
25818.m: Marie Curie did research together with Pierre Curie.

25819.q: What was Marie Curie the first woman in the world to become?
25819.e: In 1903 Marie Curie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize.
25819.m: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

25820.q: Which rays did Marie Curie study?
25820.e: Marie Curie studied substances that give off rays on their own. She coined the word “radioactive” for them.

25821.q: Which country did Louis Pasteur come from?
25821.e: Louis Pasteur was born in France in 1822. He later worked in Paris.

25822.q: Against which disease did Louis Pasteur develop a vaccine for humans?
25822.e: In 1885 Pasteur vaccinated a little boy who had been bitten by a rabid animal. The boy stayed healthy.
25822.m: Louis Pasteur developed a vaccine against rabies.

25823.q: Which animal had bitten the boy Joseph Meister before Pasteur vaccinated him?
25823.e: A rabid dog had bitten the boy. Thanks to Pasteur’s vaccine, he did not get rabies.
25823.m: Joseph Meister was bitten by a rabid dog.

25824.q: What do you do to milk when pasteurising it?
25824.e: The milk is heated briefly. This kills many germs and the milk stays fresh longer.
25824.m: Pasteurised milk has been heated briefly.

25825.q: What happens when milk is pasteurised?
a: It is heated briefly to kill germs
All the fat is filtered out
25825.e: When milk is pasteurised, it is heated briefly. This kills most of the germs and the milk stays fresh longer. The process is named after Louis Pasteur.
25825.m: Pasteurising means heating briefly so that the germs die.

25826.q: As Louis Pasteur showed, what makes food go off?
25826.e: Pasteur proved that tiny living things such as bacteria make food go off. You can only see them with a microscope. Cold, salt and sugar, on the other hand, make food keep longer.
25826.m: Tiny germs make food go off.

25827.e: With a vaccination, the body learns to defend itself against a germ that causes disease. Then you get ill less often or less seriously.

25828.q: Who carried out the first smallpox vaccination, even before Pasteur?
25828.e: In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner vaccinated against smallpox. Pasteur later built on this idea.
25828.m: Edward Jenner carried out the first smallpox vaccination.

25829.q: In which city is the famous Pasteur Institute?
25829.e: The Pasteur Institute opened in Paris in 1888. Research into diseases and vaccines is still carried out there today.
25829.m: The Pasteur Institute is in Paris.

25830.e: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in his laboratory in London. It has saved millions of lives since then.

25831.q: Which country did Alexander Fleming come from?
25831.e: Alexander Fleming was born in Scotland in 1881. He later worked as a researcher in London.

25832.e: Penicillin is produced by a mould. The mould is called Penicillium.

25833.e: Fleming went on holiday and left dishes of bacteria standing. When he came back, mould was growing on them and had killed the bacteria.

25834.q: Against which germs does penicillin help?
25834.e: Penicillin kills bacteria or stops them growing. It does not help against viruses, for example with flu.

25835.q: What are medicines like penicillin called?
25835.e: Penicillin is one of the antibiotics. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “against life”.

25836.q: In which year did Fleming discover penicillin?
25836.e: Alexander Fleming made his discovery in London in 1928.

25837.q: Which famous prize did Fleming receive in 1945 for penicillin?
25837.e: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945. He shared it with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.
25837.m: Fleming received the Nobel Prize for penicillin.

25838.q: Which country did Charles Darwin come from?
25838.e: Charles Darwin was born in England in 1809. He was a famous naturalist.

25839.q: Which ship did Darwin sail around the world on?
25839.e: From 1831 to 1836 Darwin sailed around the world on the ship HMS Beagle. Beagle is also the name of a dog breed.
25839.m: Darwin sailed around the world on the Beagle.

25840.q: In which ocean are the Galápagos Islands?
25840.e: The Galápagos Islands are in the Pacific Ocean, west of South America.
25840.m: The Galápagos Islands are in the Pacific.

25841.q: Which country do the Galápagos Islands belong to?
25841.e: The Galápagos Islands belong to Ecuador in South America. They lie about 1,000 kilometres off the coast.
25841.m: The Galápagos Islands belong to Ecuador.

25842.q: Which huge animals live on the Galápagos Islands?
25842.e: Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands. The islands are even named after them, because “galápago” is an old Spanish word for tortoise.
25842.m: Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands.

25843.q: Which birds on the Galápagos Islands are named after Darwin?
25843.e: The finches on the Galápagos Islands have differently shaped beaks depending on their food. Today they are called Darwin’s finches.
25843.m: Darwin’s finches have differently shaped beaks.

25844.q: What did Darwin describe with his famous theory?
25844.e: Darwin explained that animals and plants change over a very long time. This is called evolution.
25844.m: Darwin explained the evolution of living things.

25845.q: Which special lizards swim in the sea around the Galápagos Islands?
25845.e: Marine iguanas dive in the sea and eat seaweed. They are only found on the Galápagos Islands.
25845.m: Marine iguanas dive in the sea for seaweed.

25846.q: In which Swiss city did Einstein work at the patent office?
25846.e: From 1902 Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern. Today you can visit the Einstein House in Bern.
25846.m: Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern.

25847.q: At which university in Zurich did Einstein study?
25847.e: Einstein studied at ETH in Zurich, then called the Polytechnic. He trained as a teacher of maths and physics.

25848.q: In which country was Albert Einstein born?
25848.e: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm in Germany in 1879.
25848.m: Albert Einstein was born in Germany.

25849.e: The formula E = mc² shows that mass and energy are connected. Einstein published it in 1905.
25849.m: Einstein’s most famous formula links mass and energy.

25850.q: What is Einstein’s most famous theory called?
25850.e: Einstein developed the theory of relativity. It explains space, time and gravity in a new way.
25850.m: Einstein developed the theory of relativity.

25851.q: Which citizenship did Einstein receive in 1901?
25851.e: Einstein became a Swiss citizen in 1901. He kept his Swiss citizenship all his life.
25851.m: Einstein was also a Swiss citizen.

25852.q: Which musical instrument did Einstein like to play?
25852.e: Einstein played the violin from childhood. Music helped him think.
25852.m: Einstein liked to play the violin.

25853.q: What is the photo of Einstein looking into the camera famous for?
a: He is sticking his tongue out
He is sitting on a horse
25853.e: On his birthday in 1951, Einstein stuck his tongue out at a photographer. The picture became world-famous.
25853.m: In a famous photo, Einstein is sticking his tongue out.

25854.e: Florence Nightingale was a nurse. She turned nursing into a proper profession.

25855.q: What nickname did Florence Nightingale have?
25855.e: At night she walked through the hospital with a lamp and checked on the wounded. That is why she was called “the Lady with the Lamp”.
25855.m: Florence Nightingale was called the Lady with the Lamp.

25856.q: Which city was Florence Nightingale named after?
25856.e: Florence was born in Florence in Italy in 1820, and she was named after the city.
25856.m: Florence Nightingale was named after the city of Florence.

25857.q: What was especially important to Florence Nightingale in hospital?
25857.e: She made sure there were clean beds, fresh air and water for washing. She was convinced that dirt made many of the wounded ill.
25857.m: Florence Nightingale made sure hospitals were clean.

25858.q: Whom did Florence Nightingale care for in the Crimean War?
25858.e: In the Crimean War, from 1854, she and other women cared for wounded British soldiers.
25858.m: Florence Nightingale cared for wounded soldiers.

25859.q: What did Florence Nightingale found in London in 1860?
25859.e: In 1860 she founded a school for nurses in London. There women learned nursing as a profession.
25859.m: Florence Nightingale founded a school for nurses.

25860.q: Which day falls on Florence Nightingale’s birthday?
25860.e: She was born on 12 May. On this day, International Nurses Day is celebrated around the world.

25861.q: How did Florence Nightingale show what the soldiers were dying of?
25861.e: She counted the deaths and drew coloured diagrams. In this way she convinced the government to improve the hospitals.
25861.m: Florence Nightingale showed her figures with diagrams.

25862.e: Robert Koch was a German doctor. Although “Koch” means “cook” in German, he was not a cook but a researcher of bacteria.
25862.m: Robert Koch was a doctor and bacteria researcher.

25863.q: Which country did Robert Koch come from?
25863.e: Robert Koch was born in Germany in 1843. He later worked in Berlin.

25864.q: Which germ did Robert Koch discover in 1882?
25864.e: In 1882 Koch found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. At the time it was one of the most common causes of death.
25864.m: Robert Koch discovered the germ that causes tuberculosis.

25865.q: Which instrument did Robert Koch use to look for bacteria?
25865.e: Bacteria are so small that you can only see them with a microscope. Koch stained them so they were easier to recognise.
25865.m: Robert Koch studied bacteria with the microscope.

25866.q: Which organ does tuberculosis usually attack?
25866.e: Tuberculosis usually affects the lungs. People who are ill often cough hard for a long time.

25867.q: Which disease did Koch study in Egypt and India in 1883?
25867.e: Koch travelled to Egypt and India and found the germ that causes cholera there. This disease spreads through dirty water.
25867.m: Robert Koch found the germ that causes cholera.

25868.q: Which prize did Robert Koch receive in 1905?
25868.e: Robert Koch received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1905. He was one of the most important bacteria researchers of his time.
25868.m: Robert Koch received the Nobel Prize in 1905.

25869.q: Which disease-causing germ did Robert Koch discover in 1882?
25869.e: In 1882 Robert Koch presented the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. He later received the Nobel Prize for this.
25869.m: Robert Koch discovered the germ that causes tuberculosis.

25870.e: Röntgen discovered rays that pass through the body. In English they are called X-rays; in German they are named after him.

25871.q: In which year did Röntgen discover his rays?
25871.e: Röntgen made his discovery in Würzburg in November 1895.

25872.q: What can you see especially clearly on an X-ray image?
25872.e: X-rays pass easily through skin and muscles, but not through bones. That is why the bones show up clearly.
25872.m: On an X-ray image you can see the bones.

25873.q: Whose hand is shown in one of the first X-ray images?
25873.e: Röntgen X-rayed the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha. You can see her bones and her ring.
25873.m: One of the first X-ray images shows Röntgen’s wife’s hand.

25874.q: What did Röntgen himself call his rays?
25874.e: Röntgen called them “X-rays” because they were unknown. In English they are still called that today.

25875.q: In which Swiss city did Röntgen study?
25875.e: Röntgen studied mechanical engineering in Zurich and also got his doctorate there.

25876.q: Which prize did Röntgen become the first to receive in 1901?
25876.e: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901. Röntgen received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
25876.m: Röntgen received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.

25877.q: When do you often need an X-ray at the doctor’s?
25877.e: With an X-ray image, the doctor can see whether and where a bone is broken.
25877.m: An X-ray image shows a broken bone.

25878.q: Which country did Ada Lovelace come from?
25878.e: Ada Lovelace was born in London, the capital of England.

25879.q: What was Ada Lovelace especially gifted at?
25879.e: Ada Lovelace had lots of maths lessons from childhood. She became a well-known mathematician.

25880.q: What did Ada Lovelace write as one of the first people ever?
25880.e: In 1843 she wrote precise step-by-step instructions for a machine. Many people see this as the first computer program.
25880.m: Ada Lovelace wrote an early computer program.

25881.q: Which inventor did Ada Lovelace work with?
25881.e: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician and inventor. Ada Lovelace described all the things his machine could do.
25881.m: Ada Lovelace worked with Charles Babbage.

25882.e: Her father was the English poet Lord Byron. Her mother mainly encouraged her maths.
25882.m: Ada Lovelace’s father was the poet Lord Byron.

25883.q: What is named after Ada Lovelace?
25883.e: The programming language “Ada” bears her name. This honours her as a computer pioneer.
25883.m: A programming language is named after Ada Lovelace.

25884.q: Which noble title did Ada Lovelace get through her marriage?
25884.e: Ada married William King. He became Earl of Lovelace in 1838, so she was the Countess of Lovelace.

25885.q: In which century did Ada Lovelace live?
25885.e: Ada Lovelace lived from 1815 to 1852. That is in the 19th century, long before today’s computers.
25885.m: Ada Lovelace lived in the 19th century.

25886.q: Which kind of electricity did Nikola Tesla become famous for?
25886.e: Tesla championed alternating current. With it, electricity can be sent well over long distances.
25886.m: Nikola Tesla made alternating current well known.

25887.q: Which country did Tesla emigrate to in 1884?
25887.e: In 1884 Tesla moved to New York in the USA. There he made his most important inventions.
25887.m: Nikola Tesla emigrated to the USA.

25888.q: Which famous inventor did Tesla work for briefly in the USA?
25888.e: Tesla worked for Thomas Edison for a short time. Afterwards the two argued about which kind of electric current was better.
25888.m: Tesla worked briefly for Thomas Edison.

25889.q: Which electrical machine is named after Tesla?
25889.e: The Tesla coil produces very high voltages. It creates artificial lightning.
25889.m: The Tesla coil makes artificial lightning.

25890.q: At which famous waterfalls did Tesla help build a power station using alternating current?
25890.e: In 1895 a large hydroelectric power station started working at Niagara Falls. Its generators were based on Tesla's inventions.
25890.m: At Niagara Falls, electricity was made using Tesla's idea.

25891.q: Which birds did Tesla especially like to feed in New York?
25891.e: Tesla fed lots of pigeons in New York. He loved these birds very much.

25892.q: In which present-day country was Tesla born?
25892.e: Tesla was born in 1856 in the village of Smiljan. It is in what is now Croatia.
25892.m: Nikola Tesla was born in what is now Croatia.

25893.q: What is the tesla in physics?
25893.e: The tesla is a unit used to measure the strength of magnetic fields. It was named after Nikola Tesla.
25893.m: The tesla is a unit for magnetic fields.

25894.q: Which plants did Gregor Mendel use for his experiments?
25894.e: From 1856 to 1863 Mendel grew many thousands of pea plants and watched them closely.
25894.m: Gregor Mendel did his research with peas.

25895.e: Gregor Mendel was a monk at the monastery in Brno. Later he even became its abbot.

25896.q: Where did Mendel grow his peas?
25896.e: Mendel used the garden of his monastery in Brno for his experiments.
25896.m: Mendel grew his peas in the monastery garden.

25897.q: What did Mendel want to find out with his peas?
a: How to protect peas from pests
25897.e: Mendel wanted to know how parents pass on their features to their offspring. In this way he discovered rules of heredity.

25898.q: What colours were the pea seeds in Mendel's experiments?
25898.e: Mendel crossed peas with yellow seeds and peas with green seeds. Then he counted the colours in their offspring.
25898.m: Mendel's peas were yellow or green.

25899.q: What are the rules that Mendel discovered called?
25899.e: The rules of heredity are named after him: Mendel's laws. Pupils learn them at school today.

25900.q: What is Gregor Mendel often called?
25900.e: Mendel was the first to find clear rules of heredity. That is why he is seen as the founder of genetics.
25900.m: Gregor Mendel is known as the father of genetics.

25901.q: In which present-day country is the city of Brno, where Mendel lived?
25901.e: In German the city is called Brünn, in Czech Brno. It is in today's Czechia.
25901.m: Mendel's monastery is in Brno in Czechia.

25902.q: Why do you get an anaesthetic for an operation?
a: So that you feel no pain
25902.e: Under general anaesthetic you sleep deeply and feel nothing. So the doctor can operate without causing pain.
25902.m: An anaesthetic stops pain during an operation.

25903.q: What does a general anaesthetic feel like for the patient?
25903.e: Under general anaesthetic you are completely unconscious. Afterwards you don't remember the operation.
25903.m: Under general anaesthetic you are in a deep sleep.

25904.q: What is the doctor who looks after the anaesthetic called?
25904.e: The anaesthetist gives the anaesthetic and watches over the patient during the whole operation.
25904.m: The anaesthetist is in charge of the anaesthetic.

25905.q: Which substance was used for a famous anaesthetic in Boston in 1846?
25905.e: In 1846 a patient in Boston was put to sleep with ether while a doctor operated on him. That was the breakthrough for anaesthesia.
25905.m: In 1846 a famous anaesthetic was given with ether.

25906.q: What were operations like before anaesthetics were invented?
25906.e: Without anaesthetic, patients felt everything. That is why surgeons had to operate as quickly as possible.
25906.m: Before anaesthetics, operations were very painful.

25907.q: Which gas did a dentist make famous in 1844 for easing pain?
25907.e: In 1844 the dentist Horace Wells had a tooth pulled out under laughing gas. Laughing gas is still sometimes used today.
25907.m: Laughing gas eases pain at the dentist.

25908.q: What does the dentist do so that only part of your mouth goes numb?
25908.e: With a local anaesthetic only a small area goes numb. You stay awake.
25908.m: With a local anaesthetic you stay awake.

25909.q: Why are you usually not allowed to eat before an anaesthetic?
a: So nothing gets into the lungs
25909.e: Under anaesthetic your protective reflexes don't work. Food from the stomach could get into the lungs. That is why your stomach must be empty.
25909.m: Before an anaesthetic your stomach must be empty.

25910.q: What is the famous book that Darwin published in 1859 called?
a: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
25910.e: In this book of 1859 Darwin explained how new species of living things come about.
25910.m: Darwin's famous book is called “On the Origin of Species”.

25911.q: How did Marie Curie help wounded soldiers in the First World War?
25911.e: Marie Curie had cars fitted with X-ray machines. This let doctors near the front find broken bones and shrapnel.
25911.m: Marie Curie brought X-ray vans to the wounded.

25912.q: Robert Koch studied bacteria. What are bacteria?
25912.e: Bacteria are so small that you can only see them with a microscope. Robert Koch found out that some bacteria make people ill.

25913.q: In which year did the Titanic sink?
25913.e: The Titanic sank during the night of 14 to 15 April 1912. It was one of the best-known shipwrecks in history.

25914.q: What did the Titanic collide with?
25914.e: The Titanic hit an iceberg in the cold North Atlantic. The hull was torn open and water poured in.
25914.m: An iceberg made the Titanic sink.

25915.q: On which voyage did the Titanic sink?
25915.e: The Titanic was brand new. It sank on its very first journey, its maiden voyage.
25915.m: A ship's first voyage is called its maiden voyage.

25916.q: In which ocean does the wreck of the Titanic lie?
25916.e: The Titanic was sailing from Europe to America across the Atlantic. It sank there and today lies about 3,800 metres deep.
25916.m: The wreck of the Titanic lies deep in the Atlantic.

25917.q: Which city was the Titanic sailing to?
25917.e: The destination of the journey was New York in America. But the Titanic never arrived there.
25917.m: The Titanic was supposed to arrive in New York.

25918.q: From which English port did the Titanic set off?
25918.e: The Titanic left Southampton in the south of England on 10 April 1912.
25918.m: The Titanic's journey began in Southampton.

25919.q: Why did so many people die when the Titanic sank?
25919.e: The lifeboats on the Titanic only had room for about half the people. Afterwards the rules were changed: every ship needs enough boats for everyone.
25919.m: A ship needs enough lifeboats for everyone on board.

25920.q: What did many people say about the Titanic before the disaster?
25920.e: The Titanic was thought to be especially safe and was often called “unsinkable”. The disaster showed that this was not true.

25921.q: Which animals often carried messages across the front in the First World War?
25921.e: Carrier pigeons always find their way back home. That is why they carried small messages when telephone lines were broken.
25921.m: In the First World War carrier pigeons carried important messages.

25922.q: In which year did the First World War end?
25922.e: Towards the end of 1918 the guns fell silent. The war was over.
25922.m: The First World War ended in 1918.

25923.q: Roughly how long did the First World War last?
25923.e: The war began in summer 1914 and lasted a little more than four years.
25923.m: The First World War lasted over four years.

25924.q: Did Switzerland fight in the First World War?
25924.e: Switzerland stayed neutral and did not take part in the fighting. But its soldiers guarded the borders.
25924.m: Switzerland stayed neutral in the First World War.

25925.q: What are the long ditches that soldiers lived in at the front called?
25925.e: The soldiers dug long ditches in the ground to protect themselves. They were often wet, cold and muddy.
25925.m: In the First World War many soldiers lived in trenches.

25926.q: In which city was the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary shot in 1914?
25926.e: The heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary was shot in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. A few weeks later the war began.
25926.m: The shots in Sarajevo led to the First World War.

25927.q: What was the name of the heir to the throne whose death started the war in 1914?
25927.e: Franz Ferdinand was supposed to become Emperor of Austria-Hungary. His murder led to the war.
25927.m: The heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand was murdered in 1914.

25928.q: On which day was the armistice signed that ended the First World War?
25928.e: On 11 November the fighting stopped. In some countries this is a day of remembrance today.
25928.m: The fighting of the First World War ended on 11 November.

25929.q: What is the Allied landing in Normandy on 6 June 1944 called?
25929.e: On 6 June 1944 many thousands of soldiers landed on the coast of France. This day is called D-Day.
25929.m: On D-Day the Allies landed in Normandy.

25930.q: In which year did the Second World War end?
25930.e: In May 1945 the war ended in Europe, and in September 1945 in Asia too.
25930.m: The Second World War ended in 1945.

25931.q: Which country did Germany attack first in 1939?
25931.e: On 1 September 1939 German soldiers marched into Poland. This was the start of the war.
25931.m: The attack on Poland was the start of the Second World War.

25932.q: Who was the dictator of Germany during the Second World War?
25932.e: Adolf Hitler ruled Germany as a dictator from 1933. He started the war and was responsible for the persecution of millions of people.
25932.m: Adolf Hitler led Germany into the Second World War.

25933.q: Who was the general of the Swiss Army in the Second World War?
25933.e: Henri Guisan led the Swiss Army from 1939 to 1945. He wanted to defend the country well.
25933.m: Henri Guisan was the Swiss general in the Second World War.

25934.q: Which country entered the war after the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941?
25934.e: In December 1941 Japan attacked the harbour of Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. After that the USA fought in the war.
25934.m: After Pearl Harbor the USA fought in the Second World War.

25935.q: On which city in Japan was the first atomic bomb dropped in 1945?
25935.e: On 6 August 1945 the USA dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. The city was almost completely destroyed.
25935.m: Hiroshima was hit by an atomic bomb in 1945.

25936.q: Who was Prime Minister of Great Britain during the Second World War?
25936.e: Winston Churchill led Great Britain through the war from 1940. He is known for his brave speeches.
25936.m: Winston Churchill led Great Britain in the Second World War.

25937.q: What did Anne Frank write in her hiding place?
25937.e: Anne Frank wrote in her diary about what she experienced, thought and felt. Today people all over the world read it.
25937.m: Anne Frank wrote a famous diary.

25938.q: In which city did Anne Frank hide with her family?
25938.e: The Frank family lived in Amsterdam in the Netherlands. They went into hiding there in 1942.

25939.q: In which city was Anne Frank born?
25939.e: Anne Frank was born in 1929 in Frankfurt am Main in Germany. Later the family moved to the Netherlands.
25939.m: Anne Frank was born in Frankfurt am Main.

25940.q: To whom did Anne Frank write the letters in her diary?
25940.e: Anne Frank imagined a friend called Kitty. Many entries begin with “Dear Kitty”.
25940.m: Anne Frank wrote her letters to her imaginary friend Kitty.

25941.q: What did Anne Frank call her family's hiding place?
25941.e: The hiding place was in a rear part of a company building. Anne called it the “Secret Annex”. Today it is a museum.
25941.m: The Frank family's hiding place was called the Secret Annex.

25942.q: Why did Anne Frank have to hide?
25942.e: The Nazis persecuted Jews and wanted to kill them. That is why the Jewish Frank family went into hiding.
25942.m: The Frank family hid because Jews were persecuted.

25943.q: Who made sure that Anne's diary was published as a book?
25943.e: Otto Frank was the only one of the family to survive. He had the diary printed in 1947.
25943.m: Anne's father Otto Frank made her diary famous.

25944.q: In which Swiss city is the Anne Frank Fonds based?
25944.e: Otto Frank later lived near Basel. In 1963 he founded the Anne Frank Fonds there, which looks after Anne's work.
25944.m: The Anne Frank Fonds is based in Basel.

25945.q: In which city are the headquarters of the UN?
25945.e: The big UN headquarters are in New York in the USA.
25945.m: The UN headquarters are in New York.

25946.q: In which Swiss city does the UN have an important seat?
25946.e: At the Palais des Nations in Geneva the UN has its largest seat in Europe. Many meetings take place there.
25946.m: The UN has a large seat in Geneva.

25947.q: What is the most important goal of the UN?
25947.e: The UN wants to prevent wars and keep the peace. It also helps people in need.
25947.m: The UN works for peace in the world.

25948.q: How many countries are members of the UN (as of 2025)?
25948.e: Almost all the countries in the world are members of the UN. In 2025 there were 193 states.
25948.m: Almost all the countries in the world belong to the UN.

25949.q: Which branches surround the world map on the UN flag?
25949.e: The light blue flag shows a white map of the world. Olive branches stand for peace.
25949.m: Olive branches are a symbol of peace.

25950.q: What are the UN's peacekeeping soldiers called because of their helmets?
25950.e: The UN's peacekeeping soldiers wear light blue helmets. That is why they are called Blue Helmets.
25950.m: The UN's peacekeepers are called Blue Helmets.

25951.q: On which day did the Berlin Wall fall?
25951.e: On the evening of 9 November the border crossings opened. Thousands of people walked across.

25952.q: Which city was divided by the Wall?
25952.e: The Wall separated East Berlin and West Berlin. Families and friends were split up.
25952.m: The Wall divided the city of Berlin.

25953.q: Why did East Germany build the Wall?
a: So that nobody could flee to the West
So that there was less noise
25953.e: Many people fled from East Germany to the West. The government wanted to stop this with the Wall.
25953.m: The Wall was meant to stop people fleeing to the West.

25954.q: In which year did Germany become one country again?
25954.e: On 3 October 1990 East Germany and West Germany became one country again. This is called reunification.

25955.q: What was the best-known border crossing in Berlin called?
25955.e: At Checkpoint Charlie foreigners and soldiers could cross between East and West. Today it is a tourist sight.
25955.m: Checkpoint Charlie was a famous border crossing in Berlin.

25956.q: Which famous gate stood right next to the Berlin Wall?
25956.e: The Brandenburg Gate stood in the closed-off area by the Wall. After the Wall fell it became a symbol of unity.
25956.m: The Brandenburg Gate is a symbol of German unity.

25957.q: Which country did Mahatma Gandhi come from?
25957.e: Gandhi was born in India in 1869. He is still a national hero there today.

25958.q: How did Gandhi fight for his goals?
25958.e: Gandhi rejected violence. He protested peacefully, for example with marches and strikes.

25959.q: Which country ruled India at that time?
25959.e: India was a British colony for a long time. Gandhi wanted India to be free.
25959.m: India belonged to Great Britain for a long time.

25960.q: Which tax did Gandhi protest against in 1930 with a long march to the sea?
25960.e: Indians were not allowed to make their own salt. Gandhi walked to the sea and made salt there himself. This was the Salt March.
25960.m: With the Salt March Gandhi protested against the salt tax.

25961.q: In which year did India become independent?
25961.e: On 15 August 1947 India became a free country.

25962.q: Which device did Gandhi use to make his own yarn for his clothes?
25962.e: Gandhi spun yarn on a spinning wheel every day. In this way he showed that Indians did not have to buy cloth from England.
25962.m: The spinning wheel became a symbol of Gandhi.

25963.q: Which international day is celebrated on Gandhi's birthday, 2 October?
25963.e: The UN declared Gandhi's birthday the International Day of Non-Violence.
25963.m: 2 October is the International Day of Non-Violence.

25964.q: In which country did Nelson Mandela become president?
25964.e: Nelson Mandela was President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. He was the country's first Black president.
25964.m: Nelson Mandela was President of South Africa.

25965.q: What did Nelson Mandela fight for?
a: Equal rights for Black and white people
25965.e: In his country Black people were treated badly and kept apart from white people. Mandela wanted everyone to be treated equally.
25965.m: Mandela fought for equal rights for everyone.

25966.q: How many years was Nelson Mandela in prison?
25966.e: Mandela was arrested in 1962 and stayed in prison for about 27 years.

25967.q: In which year was Nelson Mandela released?
25967.e: Mandela was set free in February 1990. Many people around the world were overjoyed.

25968.q: Which prize did Nelson Mandela receive in 1993?
25968.e: Mandela received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. He had worked for people to live together peacefully.
25968.m: Mandela received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

25969.q: On which island was Nelson Mandela held prisoner for many years?
25969.e: Mandela was held in the prison on Robben Island for 18 years. Today the island is a museum.
25969.m: Robben Island was Mandela's prison for a long time.

25970.q: What affectionate name do many people call Nelson Mandela?
25970.e: Madiba is the name of his clan. Many people in his home country call him that.
25970.m: Nelson Mandela is often called Madiba.

25971.q: In which country did Martin Luther King live?
25971.e: Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta in the USA in 1929 and lived there.
25971.m: Martin Luther King lived in the USA.

25972.q: Which phrase is Martin Luther King's most famous speech known for?
25972.e: He dreamed that one day all people would be treated equally.
25972.m: Martin Luther King had a dream of equality.

25973.q: In which city did Martin Luther King give his famous speech in 1963?
25973.e: In August 1963 he spoke in Washington in front of more than 200,000 people.
25973.m: The famous speech took place in Washington in 1963.

25974.q: What was Martin Luther King's job?
25974.e: Martin Luther King was the minister of a church. He also preached about justice.
25974.m: Martin Luther King was a church minister.

25975.q: What did Martin Luther King stand up for?
a: Equal rights for Black and white people
Separate schools for Black and white people
25975.e: King fought peacefully for Black people in the USA to have the same rights as white people.
25975.m: Martin Luther King fought for equal rights.

25977.q: In which year was Martin Luther King murdered?
25977.e: Martin Luther King was shot in Memphis on 4 April 1968. He was only 39 years old.

25978.q: What did Rosa Parks refuse to do on the bus?
25978.e: At that time Black people had to give up their seats for white people. Rosa Parks stayed seated and was arrested.
25978.m: Rosa Parks bravely stayed in her seat.

25979.q: In which city did Rosa Parks stay in her seat on the bus?
25979.e: Montgomery is a city in the south of the USA. Back then, Black and white people had to sit apart on buses there.
25979.m: Rosa Parks stayed in her seat on a bus in Montgomery.

25980.q: In which year did Rosa Parks refuse to stand up?
25980.e: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks stayed seated on the bus.

25981.q: What did many Black people do after Rosa Parks was arrested?
25981.e: For more than a year many people did not ride the buses. In the end they won this bus boycott.
25981.m: The Montgomery bus boycott was a great success.

25982.e: Rosa Parks worked as a seamstress in a department store. She was also active in a civil rights group.
25982.m: Rosa Parks worked as a seamstress.

25983.q: What is Rosa Parks often called?
a: Mother of the civil rights movement
25983.e: Because her courage changed so much, she is often called the “mother of the civil rights movement”.
25983.m: Rosa Parks is seen as the mother of the civil rights movement.

25984.q: What did Rosa Parks stand up for?
25984.e: Rosa Parks wanted Black and white people to have the same rights. She was very brave about it.
25984.m: Rosa Parks fought for equal rights.

25985.q: What did the suffragettes fight for?
25985.e: The suffragettes wanted women to be allowed to vote. In the past only men could.
25985.m: The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote.

25986.q: In which country were the suffragettes especially well known?
25986.e: The suffragettes in Great Britain protested loudly, with marches, posters and hunger strikes.
25986.m: The suffragettes fought for women's rights in Great Britain.

25987.q: Since which year have women in Switzerland been able to vote in national votes and elections?
25987.e: On 7 February 1971 Swiss men voted Yes at the ballot box. Compared with many countries in Europe, that was late.
25987.m: Women in Switzerland have had the vote since 1971.

25988.q: Which canton was the last to give women the vote?
25988.e: Only in 1990 did Appenzell Innerrhoden have to let women take part, after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.
25988.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden only gave women the vote in 1990.

25989.q: Who was the best-known leader of the suffragettes?
25989.e: In 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst founded a women's group that drew attention with loud protests.

25990.q: On which day did the big women's strike take place in Switzerland in 1991?
25990.e: On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women stopped working. They demanded equal rights and equal pay.
25990.m: In Switzerland 14 June is the day of the women's strike.

25991.q: In which year did women in Germany get the vote?
25991.e: Women's suffrage was introduced in Germany in November 1918. In 1919 women voted for the first time.
25991.m: Women in Germany have had the vote since 1918.

25992.q: What can women do with the right to vote?
25992.e: With the right to vote, women can help decide in popular votes and elect politicians.
25992.m: With the right to vote you can vote in ballots and elections.

25993.q: In which year was the Convention on the Rights of the Child adopted?
25993.e: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in autumn 1989.
25993.m: The Convention on the Rights of the Child has existed since 1989.

25994.q: Up to what age are you a child according to the Convention on the Rights of the Child?
25994.e: Everyone under 18 counts as a child. Children's rights apply to them.
25994.m: Children's rights apply to everyone under 18.

25995.q: Since which year has the Convention on the Rights of the Child applied in Switzerland?
25995.e: Switzerland joined the Convention in 1997. Since then children's rights have officially applied here too.
25995.m: The Convention on the Rights of the Child has applied in Switzerland since 1997.

25996.q: Which right is one of the children's rights?
a: The right to a mobile phone
25996.e: Every child has the right to go to school and learn.
25996.m: Every child has a right to education.

25997.q: Does every child have a right to play and free time?
a: Yes, that is a children's right
25997.e: Play, rest and free time are clearly stated children's rights.

25998.q: What is the UN's children's fund called?
25998.e: UNICEF helps children all over the world, for example with food, vaccinations and schools.
25998.m: UNICEF is the UN's children's fund.

25999.q: What does every child have a right to straight after birth?
25999.e: Every child should be given a name and be registered straight after birth.
25999.m: Every child has a right to a name.

26000.q: How many countries belong to the European Union (as of 2025)?
26000.e: In 2025 the EU had 27 member countries.

26001.q: What is the currency of many EU countries called?
26001.e: In many EU countries people pay with the euro. There are coins and notes.
26001.m: Many EU countries pay with the euro.

26002.q: Is Switzerland a member of the European Union?
26002.e: Switzerland is not in the EU. But it has many agreements with the EU.
26002.m: Switzerland does not belong to the EU.

26003.q: How many gold stars are there on the European flag?
26003.e: Twelve gold stars stand in a circle on the blue background. The number always stays the same.
26003.m: The European flag has twelve gold stars.

26004.q: In which city are many EU offices based?
26004.e: The European Commission and the Council of the EU work in Brussels in Belgium.
26004.m: Many EU offices are in Brussels.

26005.q: Which country left the EU in 2020?
26005.e: The United Kingdom left on 31 January 2020. This is called Brexit.
26005.m: With Brexit the United Kingdom left the EU.

26006.q: On which day does the EU celebrate Europe Day?
26006.e: On 9 May 1950 Robert Schuman proposed close cooperation in Europe. Europe Day remembers this.
26006.m: The EU's Europe Day is on 9 May.

26008.e: Sputnik 1 was the first satellite built by people to circle the Earth.
26008.m: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite.

26009.q: Which country sent Sputnik 1 into space?
26009.e: The Soviet Union was a large state that included Russia. It launched Sputnik 1.
26009.m: Sputnik 1 came from the Soviet Union.

26010.q: In which year did Sputnik 1 go into space?
26010.e: Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 October 1957. This was the start of the space age.
26010.m: Space travel began in 1957 with Sputnik 1.

26011.e: Sputnik 1 was a shiny metal ball, about the size of a beach ball.

26012.q: How many long antennas did Sputnik 1 have?
26012.e: Four long rod antennas were attached to the ball.

26013.q: What did Sputnik 1 send to Earth?
26013.e: Sputnik 1 sent simple beeping sounds. Radio amateurs all over the world could hear them.
26013.m: Sputnik 1 beeped to Earth by radio.

26014.q: What does the Russian word “Sputnik” mean?
26014.e: In Russian “sputnik” means companion or fellow traveller. The satellite travels along with the Earth.

26015.q: What happened to Sputnik 1 in the end?
a: It burned up in the air.
26015.e: After about three months Sputnik 1 sank lower and burned up in the Earth's atmosphere.
26015.m: Sputnik 1 burned up in the atmosphere in the end.

26016.q: What kind of animal was Laika?
26016.e: Laika was a small female dog. She was chosen for a flight into space.

a: the first animal to orbit the Earth
the first dog on the Moon
the first animal on Mount Everest
the first dog at the South Pole
26017.e: Laika was the first living creature to fly in an orbit around the Earth.
26017.m: Laika was the first animal to orbit the Earth.

26018.q: In which spacecraft did Laika fly?
26018.e: Laika flew in Sputnik 2, a satellite with a small cabin for the dog.

26019.q: In which year did Laika fly into space?
26019.e: Sputnik 2 with Laika on board was launched on 3 November 1957.

26020.q: Where did Laika live before she was chosen for space travel?
26020.e: Laika was a stray dog from Moscow. People thought such dogs were used to cold and hunger.
26020.m: Laika was a street dog from Moscow.

26021.q: Did Laika come back to Earth alive?
26021.e: A return was not possible. Laika died a few hours after the launch because the cabin got too hot.
26021.m: Laika did not return to Earth.

26022.q: Why was Laika sent into space?
a: to test whether living things could survive the flight
26022.e: Before people were allowed to fly, scientists wanted to know whether a living creature could survive the launch and floating in space.
26022.m: Laika helped test whether living things can fly into space.

26023.q: Who was the first person in space?
26023.e: Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union was the first person to fly into space.
26023.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space.

26024.q: What are space travellers from Russia, like Yuri Gagarin, called?
26024.e: In Russia, and earlier in the Soviet Union, space travellers are called cosmonauts. In the USA they say astronauts.
26024.m: Russian space travellers are called cosmonauts.

26025.q: What was the name of Yuri Gagarin's spacecraft?
26025.e: Gagarin flew in the space capsule Vostok 1. “Vostok” means east.

26026.q: How many times did Yuri Gagarin go around the Earth?
26026.e: Gagarin flew exactly one lap around the Earth and then landed again.
26026.m: Gagarin went around the Earth once.

26027.q: Roughly how long did Gagarin's flight last?
26027.e: The flight lasted about 108 minutes, so just under two hours.
26027.m: Gagarin's flight lasted just under two hours.

26028.q: What does Gagarin's shout at take-off, “Poyekhali!”, mean?
26028.e: At take-off Gagarin shouted “Poyekhali!” in Russian. It means roughly “Let's go!”.

26029.q: What was Yuri Gagarin's job before his space flight?
26029.e: Gagarin was a pilot in the air force and flew fast fighter planes.
26029.m: Yuri Gagarin was a fighter pilot before.

26030.q: How did Yuri Gagarin get back to the ground in the end?
26030.e: Shortly before landing, Gagarin got out of the capsule and floated down to Earth on a parachute.

26031.q: How many astronauts flew on Apollo 11?
26031.e: The crew was made up of three astronauts. Two of them walked on the Moon.
26031.m: Apollo 11 had three astronauts on board.

26032.q: Where did the Apollo 11 capsule land when it returned to Earth?
26032.e: The capsule came down on parachutes into the Pacific Ocean. A ship picked up the astronauts.
26032.m: Apollo 11 landed in the Pacific on its return.

26033.q: Which astronaut stayed in the spacecraft and orbited the Moon?
26033.e: Michael Collins waited in the command module while his two colleagues were on the Moon.
26033.m: Michael Collins stayed in the spacecraft above the Moon.

26034.q: Which astronaut was the second to step onto the Moon?
26034.e: Buzz Aldrin climbed out of the lunar module shortly after his commander.
26034.m: Buzz Aldrin was the second person on the Moon.

26035.q: What did the Apollo 11 astronauts bring back from the Moon?
26035.e: They brought back just over 20 kilograms of rock and dust from the Moon. Scientists are still studying them today.
26035.m: Apollo 11 brought Moon rock to Earth.

26036.q: Which rocket did Apollo 11 launch on?
26036.e: The huge Saturn V rocket sent the astronauts on their way to the Moon.
26036.m: Apollo 11 launched on the Saturn V rocket.

26037.q: What is the flat plain on the Moon where Neil Armstrong landed called?
26037.e: The dark plains on the Moon are called seas, even though there is no water there. Armstrong landed in the Sea of Tranquillity.
26037.m: Armstrong landed in the Sea of Tranquillity.

26038.q: What was Neil Armstrong's job before space travel?
26038.e: Armstrong flew new, very fast aeroplanes to test them.
26038.m: Neil Armstrong was a test pilot.

26039.q: How does Armstrong's famous sentence continue: “That's one small step for man, one ... leap for mankind”?
26039.e: Armstrong meant that his small step was something very big for all people.
26039.m: Armstrong spoke of a giant leap for mankind.

26040.q: Why do Armstrong's footprints stay on the Moon for a long time?
a: The ground is made of concrete.
26040.e: There is no air on the Moon, so there is no wind or rain to wipe away the prints.
26040.m: Without wind, footprints on the Moon last a long time.

26041.q: Roughly how long was Neil Armstrong outside on the Moon?
26041.e: Armstrong spent about two and a half hours outside the lunar module.
26041.m: Armstrong was outside on the Moon for about two and a half hours.

26042.q: Which flag did Armstrong and his colleague put up on the Moon?
26042.e: The Moon landing was a project of the USA. That is why the astronauts put up the US flag.
26042.m: There is a US flag on the Moon.

26043.q: How were many people able to watch Armstrong's first step live?
26043.e: Hundreds of millions of people watched on television. There was no internet and there were no mobile phones back then.
26043.m: The Moon landing was shown live on television.

26044.q: In which year did Valentina Tereshkova fly into space?

26045.q: Tereshkova's radio call sign was “Chaika”. Which bird is that?
26045.e: “Chaika” is the Russian word for seagull.

26046.q: Which sport did Valentina Tereshkova do before her flight?
26046.e: She was an experienced parachutist. That was important, because she had to jump out with a parachute for the landing.

26047.q: Where did Valentina Tereshkova work before she became a cosmonaut?
26047.e: She worked in a factory where cloth was made.
26047.m: Tereshkova first worked in a textile factory.

26048.q: How long was Valentina Tereshkova in space?
26048.e: She was up there for almost 71 hours and orbited the Earth 48 times.
26048.m: Tereshkova was in space for almost three days.

26049.q: How many people were in Tereshkova's space capsule?
26049.e: She flew completely alone. To this day she is the only woman who has been in space on her own.
26049.m: Tereshkova flew into space all alone.

26050.q: What was special about the Space Shuttle?
26050.e: The Space Shuttle's orbiter could be used again after landing and flew many times.
26050.m: The Space Shuttle could fly several times.

26051.q: How did the Space Shuttle land?
a: like an aeroplane on a runway
26051.e: The Shuttle had wings and glided back to Earth. It landed on a long runway like an aeroplane.
26051.m: The Space Shuttle landed like an aeroplane.

26052.q: Which space agency built the Space Shuttle?
26052.e: The Space Shuttle was a spacecraft of NASA, the space agency of the USA.
26052.m: The Space Shuttle belonged to NASA.

26053.q: In which year did the first Space Shuttle fly?
26053.e: The first flight, with the Shuttle “Columbia”, took place in April 1981.
26053.m: The Space Shuttle first flew in 1981.

26054.q: In which year did the last Space Shuttle fly?
26054.e: The last flight took place in 2011 with the Shuttle “Atlantis”.
26054.m: The Space Shuttle flew for the last time in 2011.

26055.q: Which of these was the name of a Space Shuttle?
26055.e: The Shuttles were called Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour.
26055.m: Atlantis was one of the Space Shuttles.

26056.q: Which Swiss man flew into space on the Space Shuttle several times?
26056.e: Claude Nicollier from the canton of Vaud flew on the Space Shuttle four times. So far he is the only Swiss astronaut to have been in space.
26056.m: Claude Nicollier flew into space on the Space Shuttle.

26057.q: What colour was the Space Shuttle's large external tank?
26057.e: The large fuel tank was orange because it was not painted.
26057.m: The Space Shuttle's external tank was orange.

26058.q: How long does the ISS take to go once around the Earth?
26058.e: The ISS is very fast and goes around the Earth in about an hour and a half.
26058.m: The ISS goes around the Earth in about 90 minutes.

26059.q: Roughly how many sunrises does the ISS crew see in one day?
26059.e: Because the ISS orbits the Earth about 16 times a day, you see about 16 sunrises.
26059.m: On the ISS you see about 16 sunrises a day.

26060.q: Can you see the ISS from Earth?
a: Yes, as a bright dot in the sky.
26060.e: In the evening or morning you can see the ISS as a bright dot moving quickly across the sky.
26060.m: You can see the ISS as a bright dot in the night sky.

26061.q: How do the astronauts sleep on the ISS?
a: in a sleeping bag fixed in place
26061.e: So that they don't float around, they sleep in sleeping bags attached to the wall.
26061.m: On the ISS you sleep in a sleeping bag fixed in place.

26062.q: What is it called when you float freely in the ISS?
26062.e: On the ISS you feel no weight and you float. This is called weightlessness.
26062.m: On the ISS there is weightlessness.

26063.q: Since which year have people lived on the ISS all the time?
26063.e: The first crew moved in in November 2000. Since then the ISS has always been occupied.
26063.m: People have always lived on the ISS since 2000.

26064.q: Which space organisation, which Switzerland is also part of, is involved in the ISS?
26064.e: Switzerland is a member of the European Space Agency, ESA. ESA has its own laboratory on the ISS.
26064.m: Through ESA, Switzerland is also involved in the ISS.

26065.q: Who was the first person to reach the South Pole?
26065.e: Roald Amundsen and his companions were the first to arrive at the South Pole.
26065.m: Roald Amundsen was the first at the South Pole.

26066.q: Which country did Roald Amundsen come from?
26066.e: Amundsen was a polar explorer from Norway.

26067.q: In which year did Amundsen reach the South Pole?
26067.e: In 1911 Amundsen became the first person to stand at the South Pole.
26067.m: Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911.

26068.e: Amundsen relied on sledge dogs. They moved very well over ice and snow.
26068.m: Sledge dogs pulled Amundsen to the South Pole.

26069.q: What was the name of the ship in which Amundsen sailed to Antarctica?
26069.e: Amundsen sailed on the “Fram”. In Norwegian the word means “forward”.
26069.m: Amundsen's ship was called the Fram.

26070.q: Which explorer reached the South Pole shortly after Amundsen?
26070.e: The British explorer Robert Scott reached the Pole about a month later. Shackleton and Nansen never reached the South Pole, and Peary explored near the North Pole.
26070.m: Robert Scott reached the South Pole after Amundsen.

26071.q: In which month did Amundsen reach the South Pole?
26071.e: In December it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere. That is when it is least cold in Antarctica.
26071.m: Amundsen was at the South Pole in December.

26072.q: Who were the first to stand on the summit of Mount Everest?
26072.e: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the highest summit in the world together.
26072.m: Hillary and Tenzing were the first to climb Mount Everest.

26073.q: In which year was Mount Everest climbed for the first time?
26073.e: On 29 May 1953 people stood on the summit for the first time.
26073.m: Mount Everest was first climbed in 1953.

26074.e: According to the 2020 measurement, Mount Everest is 8,849 metres high. It is the highest mountain on Earth.

26075.q: In which mountain range is Mount Everest?
26075.e: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and China.
26075.m: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas.

26076.q: Which country did Edmund Hillary come from?
26076.e: Edmund Hillary was a mountaineer and beekeeper from New Zealand.
26076.m: Edmund Hillary came from New Zealand.

26077.q: Which mountain people did Tenzing Norgay belong to?
26077.e: The Sherpa live in the Himalayas and are very experienced mountaineers.

26078.q: What did Hillary and Tenzing take with them to breathe better in the thin air?
26078.e: Right at the top the air is very thin. With oxygen from bottles they could breathe better.
26078.m: Hillary and Tenzing breathed oxygen from bottles.

26079.q: Which country sent an expedition in 1952 that almost reached the summit of Mount Everest?
26079.e: In 1952 a Swiss expedition got to about 250 metres below the summit. A year later the first ascent succeeded.
26079.m: Swiss climbers almost reached the top of Mount Everest in 1952.

26080.q: In which city was Auguste Piccard born?
26080.e: Auguste Piccard was born in Basel in 1884.

26081.q: In what did Auguste Piccard fly higher than anyone before him?
26081.e: Piccard flew in a huge gas balloon higher than any person before him.
26081.m: Auguste Piccard flew very high in a balloon.

26082.q: Where did Auguste Piccard fly in a balloon in 1931, as one of the first people ever?
26082.e: On 27 May 1931 Piccard rose into the stratosphere in his balloon. That is a layer of air high above the clouds.
26082.m: In 1931 Piccard flew into the stratosphere in a balloon.

26083.q: Roughly how high did Auguste Piccard rise on his first balloon flight?
26083.e: He reached almost 15,800 metres, so about 16 kilometres. That was a world record at the time.
26083.m: Piccard rose about 16 kilometres high in the balloon.

26084.q: What did Auguste Piccard sit in on his high balloon flight?
26084.e: So high up, the air is too thin to breathe. That is why he built an airtight ball made of aluminium.
26084.m: Piccard flew in an airtight metal sphere.

26085.q: Which comic character was based on Auguste Piccard?
26085.e: The artist Hergé used Piccard as the model for Professor Calculus in “Tintin”.
26085.m: Auguste Piccard was the model for Professor Calculus.

26086.q: What did Auguste Piccard sit in on his flights into the stratosphere?
26086.e: High up, the air is very thin and cold. That is why Piccard built an airtight aluminium ball in which you could breathe. His second flight started in Dübendorf in 1932.
26086.m: Piccard flew up high in an airtight sphere.

26088.q: How was Jacques Piccard related to Auguste Piccard?
26088.e: Jacques Piccard was the son of Auguste Piccard. Together they built diving vessels.
26088.m: Jacques Piccard was the son of Auguste Piccard.

26089.q: Where did Jacques Piccard's famous record dive take him?
26089.e: He dived into the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the world's oceans.
26089.m: Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench.

26090.q: In which ocean is the Mariana Trench?
26090.e: The Mariana Trench is in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines.
26090.m: The Mariana Trench is in the Pacific.

26091.q: What was the name of Jacques Piccard's diving vessel?
26091.e: The diving vessel was called “Trieste”, after the city of Trieste, where a large part of it was built.
26091.m: Piccard's diving vessel was called the Trieste.

26092.q: Roughly how deep did Jacques Piccard dive in the Mariana Trench?
26092.e: The “Trieste” reached a depth of almost 11,000 metres. That is deeper than Mount Everest is high.

26093.q: Who dived into the Mariana Trench together with Jacques Piccard?
26093.e: Don Walsh was an officer in the American navy and dived into the depths with Piccard.
26093.m: Don Walsh dived with Jacques Piccard.

26094.q: In which year did Jacques Piccard dive into the Mariana Trench?
26094.e: The record dive took place on 23 January 1960.
26094.m: Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960.

26095.q: Which son of Jacques Piccard flew around the world in a balloon in 1999?
26095.e: In 1999 Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones flew around the Earth without stopping in the balloon “Breitling Orbiter 3”.
26095.m: Bertrand Piccard flew around the world in a balloon.

26096.e: Hubble is a telescope that circles the Earth and takes pictures of space.
26096.m: Hubble is a telescope in space.

26097.q: What is special about the Hubble telescope?
a: It orbits the Earth in space
It stands on the highest mountain
26097.e: Hubble has been orbiting the Earth since 1990. Because there is no air in the way, it takes especially sharp pictures of space.
26097.m: Hubble observes space from an orbit around the Earth.

26098.q: How was Hubble taken into space?
26098.e: The Shuttle “Discovery” carried Hubble into space in its cargo bay and released it there.
26098.m: A Space Shuttle took Hubble into space.

26099.q: Who was the Hubble telescope named after?
26099.e: Edwin Hubble was a famous astronomer from the USA. He studied distant galaxies.
26099.m: Hubble is named after an astronomer.

26100.q: Why does Hubble take sharper pictures than telescopes on Earth?
a: It is closer to the stars.
It only takes photos in the daytime.
26100.e: The Earth's air shimmers and makes pictures blurry. Hubble flies above the atmosphere.
26100.m: Without air in the way, Hubble sees especially sharply.

26101.q: What was wrong with Hubble's first pictures after the launch?
26101.e: The large mirror had been ground very slightly wrong. In 1993 astronauts fitted a correction.

26102.q: Which Swiss astronaut helped to repair Hubble in space?
26102.e: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss person in space. He worked on repair missions to Hubble.

26103.q: Roughly how big is the Hubble telescope?
a: as big as a mobile phone
26103.e: Hubble is about 13 metres long, roughly as long as a big bus.
26103.m: Hubble is about as big as a bus.

26104.q: What was the name of the inventor who built the first working programmable computer in Germany?
26104.e: Konrad Zuse built a calculating machine in Berlin that is seen as the world's first working programmable computer.
26104.m: Konrad Zuse is seen as the inventor of the computer.

26105.q: What was Konrad Zuse's most famous calculating machine called?
26105.e: Zuse named his machines with a Z and a number. The Z3 was the first one that really worked and could be programmed.
26105.m: Zuse's most famous calculating machine is called the Z3.

26106.q: What did Konrad Zuse build in Berlin in 1941?
26106.e: Zuse's calculating machine Z3 was finished in 1941. It is seen as one of the world's first freely programmable computers.
26106.m: Konrad Zuse built one of the first computers.

26107.q: Where did Konrad Zuse build his very first calculating machine, the Z1?
26107.e: From 1936 Zuse built the Z1 in his parents' living room in Berlin. The machine was mechanical and very large.
26107.m: Zuse built his first machine in his parents' living room.

26108.q: Which two digits did Zuse's Z3 machine calculate with?
26108.e: The Z3 calculated in the binary system, using only 0 and 1. Today's computers still calculate like this.
26108.m: Computers calculate with the digits 0 and 1.

26109.q: To which Swiss university was Zuse's Z4 calculating machine rented out in 1950?
26109.e: The Z4 was at ETH Zurich from 1950 to 1955. At the time it was one of the first computers working at a university in Europe.
26109.m: Zuse's Z4 did calculations at ETH Zurich for several years.

26110.q: What had Konrad Zuse trained as?
26110.e: Zuse studied civil engineering. Because he was fed up with all the long calculations, he wanted to build a machine to do them for him.
26110.m: Konrad Zuse was a civil engineer and wanted to make calculating easier.

26111.q: What was the name of a famous early large computer presented in the USA in 1946?
26111.e: ENIAC was presented in the USA in 1946. It was one of the first large electronic computers.
26111.m: ENIAC was an early large computer from the USA.

26112.q: Roughly how heavy was the early large computer ENIAC?
26112.e: ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes. That is as heavy as several elephants together.
26112.m: The large computer ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes.

26113.q: How big were the first large computers?
a: They fitted in a trouser pocket
They were as big as a book
They were as big as a shoebox
26113.e: The first large computers were huge and needed a whole room. Today a mobile phone is much more powerful.
26113.m: The first computers were as big as a whole room.

26114.q: What was inside the large computer ENIAC in their thousands?
26114.e: ENIAC had about 17,000 vacuum tubes. They got hot and often broke.
26114.m: The first large computers contained lots of tubes.

26115.q: Which animal did technicians find in a large computer that was not working properly in 1947?
26115.e: A moth had caused a fault in the computer. The technicians taped it into their logbook and wrote that they had found a real “bug”. Computer faults are still called bugs today.
26115.m: A fault in a computer program is called a bug.

26116.q: Which company became world-famous for big calculating machines and large computers?
26116.e: IBM built calculating machines early on and, from the 1950s, many large computers. They were used in companies and banks.
26116.m: For a long time IBM was the most important company for large computers.

26117.q: How did people use to feed programs and data into large computers?
26117.e: Punched cards were cardboard cards with holes in certain places. The computer read the holes as commands or numbers.
26117.m: Computers used to be fed with punched cards.

26118.q: What does the abbreviation “PC” stand for?
26118.e: PC means personal computer. That is a computer for one person, for example at home or in the office.
26118.m: A PC is a computer for one person.

26119.q: Which company did Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak found in 1976?
26119.e: Jobs and Wozniak founded Apple in California in 1976. Their first computer was the Apple I.
26119.m: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple.

26120.q: In which year did IBM bring out its first personal computer?
26120.e: The IBM PC came onto the market in 1981. It was very successful, and many other companies built similar computers.
26120.m: The IBM PC came out in 1981.

26121.q: Which device moves the pointer on the screen when you slide it across the desk?
26121.e: The computer mouse moves the pointer on the screen. It got its name because with its cable it looked like a mouse with a tail.
26121.m: You control the pointer on a computer with the mouse.

a: A portable computer that opens up
A big computer in the cellar
26122.e: A laptop is a computer with a screen, keyboard and battery all in one device. You can fold it shut and take it with you.
26122.m: A laptop is a computer you can take with you.

26123.q: Which company did Bill Gates found together with Paul Allen in 1975?
26123.e: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in 1975. The company grew very big with software for PCs, especially Windows.

26124.q: Which company, founded in Switzerland in 1981, became world-famous for computer mice?
26124.e: Logitech was founded in the canton of Vaud in 1981. Since then it has made lots of computer mice and keyboards.
26124.m: Logitech is a Swiss company for computer accessories.

26125.e: On the internet millions of computers all over the world are connected to each other. This lets them exchange data.
26125.m: The internet connects computers all over the world.

26126.q: Who used the first computer networks from which the internet later grew?
26126.e: From 1969 the ARPANET in the USA connected computers at universities and research centres. Today's internet developed from it.
26126.m: The internet began as a network of researchers and universities.

26127.q: What is the wireless connection called that lets devices at home go online without a cable?
26127.e: Wi-Fi is a wireless local network. A router sends out the signal, and a phone or laptop connects to it.
26127.m: With Wi-Fi you can go online without a cable.

26128.q: What should you do with your password?
26128.e: A password protects your accounts from strangers. Only you and perhaps your parents should know it.
26128.m: You must keep your password secret.

26129.q: What do you need a search engine on the internet for?
26129.e: A search engine searches the internet for the words you type in. Then it shows matching pages.
26129.m: With a search engine you find pages on the internet.

26130.q: What does the ending “.ch” in Swiss web addresses stand for?
26130.e: “.ch” comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. It is Switzerland's country ending.
26130.m: Swiss web addresses often end in “.ch”.

26131.q: Which three letters are at the start of many web addresses?
26131.e: “www” is short for World Wide Web. Many addresses begin with it, for example www.admin.ch.
26131.m: Many web addresses begin with www.

26132.q: What do you type in at the top of the browser to open a particular website?
26132.e: Every website has its own address. If you type it in, the page opens.
26132.m: Every website has its own web address.

26133.q: In which year was the idea for the World Wide Web first written down?
26133.e: In March 1989 a researcher wrote his proposal for a new information system. It became the Web.
26133.m: The idea for the Web dates from 1989.

a: A network covering the whole world
A cloud covering the whole world
A big map of the world
A long trip around the world
26134.e: A “web” is a network, and “world wide” means across the whole world. So it is a network that covers the world.
26134.m: The World Wide Web is a network covering the whole world.

26135.q: What is the program you use to look at websites called?
26135.e: A browser shows websites on the screen. You type in an address or click on links.
26135.m: You look at websites with a browser.

26136.q: What did CERN do with the World Wide Web technology in 1993?
a: It made it free for everyone
It sold it for a lot of money
26136.e: In 1993 CERN released the Web technology. So anyone could build websites without paying.
26136.m: The Web was made free for everyone.

26137.q: What is a link on a website?
26137.e: If you click on a link, you jump to another web page. This is how pages on the Web are connected.
26137.m: A link takes you to another web page.

26138.q: How do you say the symbol @ in English?
26138.e: In English you say “at”. So an email address means: name at provider.
26138.m: In English the symbol @ is pronounced “at”.

26139.q: Who sent the first email between two computers in 1971?
26139.e: The American Ray Tomlinson sent the first email in 1971. He connected two computers standing right next to each other.
26139.m: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email.

26140.q: What are unwanted advertising emails called?
26140.e: Spam is email you did not ask for, usually advertising. Many programs sort it out automatically.
26140.m: Unwanted advertising emails are called spam.

26141.q: What does the “e” in the word email stand for?
26141.e: Email means “electronic mail”. It is sent over the internet.

26142.q: What is an attachment in an email?
a: A file sent along with it
26142.e: You can attach files such as photos or texts to an email. The person receiving it can open them.
26142.m: With an attachment you send a file along.

26143.q: Unlike a letter, what does an email not need?
26143.e: An email travels over the internet, not by post. That is why it doesn't need a stamp.
26143.m: An email doesn't need a stamp.

26144.q: What is the job of the famous video game character Mario?
26144.e: Mario is a plumber, someone who fits water pipes. That is why he often goes through green pipes in his games.
26144.m: The game character Mario is a plumber.

26145.q: Which country does the game Tetris come from?
26145.e: Tetris was invented by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow in 1984. At that time Russia was part of the Soviet Union.
26145.m: The game Tetris comes from Russia.

26146.q: Who chases Pac-Man in the video game of the same name?
26146.e: Pac-Man eats dots in a maze. Four colourful ghosts chase him.

26147.q: Which company brought out the Game Boy in 1989?
26147.e: Nintendo's Game Boy was a small games console to take with you. It became very popular.
26147.m: The Game Boy comes from Nintendo.

26148.q: What do you usually connect a games console to at home?
26148.e: A games console shows the game on a screen. At home people usually use the television for this.
26148.m: A games console is usually connected to the television.

26149.q: What was the first home games console, which came out in 1972, called?
26149.e: The Magnavox Odyssey came out in the USA in 1972. It only showed simple dots and lines on the television.
26149.m: The first home games console was called the Magnavox Odyssey.

26150.q: Which company makes the PlayStation games console?
26150.e: The Japanese company Sony brought out the first PlayStation in 1994. Since then there have been several new models.

26151.q: In which decade was the first call made on a portable mobile phone?
26151.e: In 1973 Martin Cooper made a call on a portable phone in the street in New York. That was the start of mobile phones.
26151.m: The first mobile phone call was in 1973.

26152.q: Roughly how heavy was the first portable mobile phone from 1973?
26152.e: The first mobile phone weighed about a kilogram and was as big as a brick. Today's phones weigh much less.
26152.m: The first mobile phone was as heavy as a brick.

26153.q: What did the first text message, sent in 1992, say?
26153.e: The first text message was sent in England in December 1992. It said “Merry Christmas”.
26153.m: The first text message wished someone a merry Christmas.

26154.q: What do people in Switzerland often call a mobile phone?
26154.e: In Switzerland many people call a mobile phone a “Natel”. That used to be the name of the mobile network of the Swiss PTT.
26154.m: In Switzerland a mobile phone is often called a Natel.

26155.q: Where were the first mobile phones in Switzerland built in from 1978?
26155.e: The first mobile phones were so big and heavy that they were fixed into cars. That is why they were called car phones.
26155.m: The first mobile phones were car phones.

26156.q: What could you mainly do with the first mobile phones?
26156.e: The first mobile phones could only make calls. Cameras, internet and apps only came many years later.
26156.m: With the first mobile phones you could only make calls.

26157.q: Which emergency number can you dial on a mobile phone all over Europe?
26157.e: The number 112 works all over Europe, including Switzerland. 117, 118 and 144 are emergency numbers only for Switzerland.

26158.q: What is a screen that reacts when you touch it with your finger called?
26158.e: A touchscreen is a screen you touch to control it. Almost all smartphones have one.
26158.m: A touchscreen reacts when you touch it.

26159.q: How do you usually operate a smartphone?
a: With your finger on the screen
26159.e: You tap and swipe with your finger directly on the screen.
26159.m: You operate a smartphone with your finger.

26160.q: What does the word “smart” in “smartphone” mean?
26160.e: “Smart” means clever. A smartphone can do much more than just make calls.
26160.m: A smartphone is a clever phone.

26161.q: What does the GPS in a smartphone show?
26161.e: GPS receives signals from satellites. That is how the smartphone works out its location, for example for a map.
26161.m: With GPS the smartphone knows where you are.

26162.q: What is Google's operating system that runs on many smartphones called?
26162.e: Android is Google's operating system. It runs on smartphones from many different makers.

26163.q: Which device is NOT built into a normal smartphone?
26163.e: A smartphone has a camera, calculator and clock built in. But it can only print with a separate printer.
26163.m: A smartphone combines many devices in one.

26164.q: What does a digital camera store its photos on?
26164.e: Digital cameras store photos as data on a small memory card. Older cameras needed a film for this.
26164.m: Digital photos are stored on a memory card.

a: A tiny dot in a picture
26165.e: A digital picture is made of lots of tiny coloured dots. These dots are called pixels.
26165.m: A digital picture is made of many pixels.

26166.q: At which company did Steven Sasson build the first digital camera in 1975?
26166.e: Steven Sasson worked at Kodak when he built the first digital camera in 1975. It was as big as a toaster.
26166.m: The first digital camera was made at Kodak.

26167.q: What did the picture from the first digital camera of 1975 look like?
26167.e: The first digital camera only took small black and white pictures. It needed more than 20 seconds to save one picture.
26167.m: The first digital photo was black and white.

26168.q: What is a big advantage of a digital camera over a film camera?
a: You can see the photo straight away
26168.e: With a digital camera you see the photo on the screen at once. With film, the pictures first had to be developed.
26168.m: You can look at digital photos straight away.

26169.q: How many dots are there in one megapixel?
26169.e: “Mega” means million. So one megapixel is a million dots.
26169.m: One megapixel is a million dots.

26170.q: What do you “fill up” an electric car with?
26170.e: An electric car runs on an electric motor. You charge the electricity for it from a socket or charging station.
26170.m: An electric car runs on electricity.

26171.q: Where does an electric car store its electricity?
26171.e: A large battery, usually under the floor of the car, stores the electricity. It is filled up again when you charge it.
26171.m: The electricity in an electric car is in the battery.

26172.q: Unlike a petrol car, what does an electric car not have?
26172.e: An electric car doesn't burn any fuel. So there are no exhaust fumes, and it doesn't need an exhaust pipe.
26172.m: An electric car has no exhaust pipe.

26173.q: How long have electric cars existed?
26173.e: Around 1900 there were already lots of electric cars on the roads. Later petrol cars became more popular because they could go further.
26173.m: Electric cars already existed more than 100 years ago.

26174.q: Where do you charge an electric car when you are out and about?
26174.e: Charging stations are at car parks, motorway services and petrol stations. You plug a cable into the car there.
26174.m: You charge electric cars at charging stations.

26175.q: Why do new electric cars make a special noise when driving slowly?
a: So that pedestrians can hear them
26175.e: Electric cars are very quiet. An artificial sound warns pedestrians and cyclists so they notice the car.
26175.m: Electric cars make a sound to protect pedestrians.

26176.q: What does a hybrid car have?
a: An electric motor and a petrol engine
26176.e: “Hybrid” means mixed. A hybrid car has two drives: an electric motor and a combustion engine.
26176.m: A hybrid car has two different motors.

26177.q: Where does solar energy come from?
26177.e: “Sol” is the Latin word for sun. Solar energy is energy from sunlight.
26177.m: Solar energy is energy from the Sun.

26178.q: What are the parts on roofs that turn sunlight into electricity called?
26178.e: Solar cells turn light directly into electricity. Many of them together make a solar panel on the roof.
26178.m: Solar cells make electricity from sunlight.

26179.q: What was the Swiss aeroplane that flew around the world in 2015 and 2016 using only solar energy called?
26179.e: Solar Impulse 2 had more than 17,000 solar cells on its wings. It flew once around the Earth without a single drop of fuel.
26179.m: Solar Impulse flew around the world using only the power of the Sun.

26180.q: Which Swiss man took turns with André Borschberg flying the solar plane around the world?
